title: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar
text: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar A cheat-map of exactly what the MPhil / MA Clinical Psychology entrances test, lifted straight from Amit Panwar's Master Guide for Clinical Psychology and folded in clean. Four parts: the exam pattern analysis (what CIP, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS hammer every year, plus the questions that actually repeat), an A–Z terminology glossary , 24 named therapies with founder + key concepts + techniques, and 25 landmark experiments with who/when/where/what. Read it once for the map, then drill the glossary and experiments cold. Source Amit Panwar, Master Guide for Clinical Psychology (Power Within Psychology). Transcribed verbatim; only obvious scan slips were cleaned. Marketing/contact pages dropped. Two of the experiments (Harlow's monkeys, the Darley "Good Samaritan / bystander" pair) appear twice in the original numbering — both kept as the guide lists them. In this guide Exam pattern analysis & repeated questions Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off A–Z terminology glossary 24 important therapies (founder · concepts · techniques) 25 landmark experiments (who · year · where · what) 1. Exam pattern analysis: what actually gets tested Admission into CIP Ranchi, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS (for MA/MPhil, PGDCP/PDCP, PsyD and PhD Clinical Psychology) is competitive, but the entrances recur in shape. The structure across institutes is similar: MCQs dominate , covering theoretical concepts, psychological tools, research methods, psychotherapies and clinical diagnosis. 1.1 Sections that show up Area What they ask General Psychology Classical theories — Freud, Jung, Adler, Skinner, Bandura; cognition, memory, sensation, perception, learning. Clinical Psychology Disorders, diagnosis, defense mechanisms, therapeutic approaches. Psychological Testing & Assessment Intelligence (Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery, Performance tests), personality, projective tests; test construction. Psychotherapy & Counselling CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred; applied / case-based. Research Methods & Statistics Design, hypothesis testing, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis. Developmental Psychology Lifespan, stage theories, attachment. Biopsychology Brain anatomy and its link to psychological function. 1.2 Commonly asked topics, with real stems A. General & Clinical Psychology. Foundational theories of Freud, Jung, Adler, Skinner, Bandura come up constantly. "Psychoanalytic theory about human personality was proposed by?" (CIP) "Insight learning is studied by?" (CIP) B. Psychometric Testing & Intelligence. Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery / Performance tests — components and Indian-context applications. "The prototype of the modern intelligence test was developed by?" (CIP) "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" (CET) Key tip Go deep on test theory and application; drill test-construction concepts ( reliability, validity ) — they're commonly tested. C. Research Methodology & Statistics. Design, hypothesis testing, and stats. Know ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis cold. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" (CIP) "What is Cronbach's Alpha used for?" (RML) D. Clinical Diagnosis & Disorders. DSM-5 criteria, especially schizophrenia, OCD, PTSD, depression; defense mechanisms; therapy approaches. "Which defense mechanism is most common in Borderline Personality Disorder?" (RINPAS) "Which therapy focuses on changing negative thought patterns?" — CBT (CIP) E. Neuropsychology & Biopsychology. Brain structures — hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, hypothalamus — and their functions. "Which structure allows communication between the hemispheres?" (RINPAS) "What is the role of the hippocampus in memory?" (NIMHANS) F. Therapies & Treatment Approaches. CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred — and applying them. "Functional Analysis is considered under which therapy?" (RINPAS) 1.3 Repeated questions across exams (use this to sharpen the mocks) Many items recur near-verbatim across papers. These are the highest-value drills. Theme Repeated stem Seen in Psychological theories "What are the basic types of defense mechanisms according to Freud?" (Id/Ego/Superego, displacement, repression) IHBAS, CIP, RML MPhil Psychometric tests "Which intelligence test includes the Pattern Drawing Test?" CET, RML Neuropsychology "Damage to the hippocampus affects?" RINPAS, NIMHANS, IHBAS Clinical disorders "Which disorder is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts?" (OCD) IHBAS, NIMHANS Defense + BPD "Which defense mechanism is most commonly associated with borderline personality disorder?" IHBAS, CIP, NIMHANS (first via UGC-NET) 1.4 Strategy for cracking the MPhil entrances Focus on core areas: master psychoanalytic, behavioural and cognitive theories; DSM-5 categories, criteria and treatments for common disorders; brain anatomy tied to cognition and memory. Practise previous-year papers: they expose recurring themes and question patterns — drill MCQs on the Bhatia Battery, CBT techniques and brain functions. Master psychometrics & research: intelligence tests, methodology and statistical tools are tested heavily; command of them is a real edge. Stay current: DSM-5 revisions and emerging trends in psychotherapy and neuropsychology. Time management: front-load high-yield topics (research methods, clinical disorders, brain functions); revise and take timed mocks to build speed and accuracy. 2. Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off One of the strongest levers for these entrances: revise UGC-NET JRF papers. The overlap with MPhil Clinical Psychology entrances is large and well-documented. High overlap of topics & questions. Clinical and abnormal psychology (schizophrenia, OCD, personality disorders and their DSM-5 criteria), psychoanalytic theory and research methodology all recur in both. "What are the key diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia?" turns up across UGC-NET, GATE and MPhil papers. Theorist items — e.g. "Which theorist proposed the collective unconscious?" — appear in MPhil exams after first showing in UGC-NET JRF. Strong focus on research methods & statistics. ANOVA, t-tests, chi-square, validity and reliability are repeated. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" appears across UGC-NET and GATE with slight variations in MPhil papers. Psychometric & intelligence tests. WAIS, Binet, and the Bhatia Battery are frequent. "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" has appeared across CIP Ranchi, UGC-NET and GATE — high repetition. Direct repeats in MPhil exams. Items on cognitive distortions, memory systems and CBT techniques carry over from UGC-NET into IHBAS, CIP and NIMHANS papers (e.g. shortlisting rounds). High-utility shared topics. Neuropsychology (hippocampus, amygdala, neurotransmitters; serotonin in depression), cognitive psychology and clinical diagnostics overlap heavily across UGC-NET JRF, GATE and MPhil. Bottom line UGC-NET JRF papers cover the same foundational topics and carry repeated questions and terminology. Folding them into your practice strengthens concepts, drills the repeats, and lifts your odds across the board. 3. A–Z terminology glossary Quick definitions for the key terms the guide flags. Searchable — type any term in the library search and this entry surfaces. A Agraphia The partial or complete inability to write, usually caused by brain damage. Aphasia Partial or complete loss of the ability to speak or comprehend language, typically caused by brain injury or neurological conditions. Aphonia The inability to produce vocal sounds due to damage to the larynx or related structures. Apraxia A disorder where an individual struggles to produce normal movement or speech despite intact muscles and comprehension. Anorexia Nervosa An eating disorder marked by an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image, leading to extreme restriction of food intake. Amygdala A structure in the brain's limbic system involved in emotion regulation, particularly fear and aggression. Anterograde Amnesia The inability to form new memories following brain damage, with preserved recall of past events. Attachment Theory Developed by John Bowlby; explains how early relationships with caregivers shape emotional bonds, with types such as secure, anxious and avoidant. Attention Span The length of time an individual can concentrate on a task without becoming distracted. Autosome Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome, carrying genetic information unrelated to sex determination. B Behavioural Theories Theories such as classical and operant conditioning that explain learning through associations, reinforcements and punishments (Pavlov, Skinner). Borderline Personality Disorder A disorder of unstable moods, relationships and behaviour, often marked by impulsive actions and intense fears of abandonment. Broca's Area A frontal-lobe region responsible for speech production; damage results in Broca's aphasia. Brute Force A problem-solving strategy that tries all possible solutions until the correct one is found. C Catharsis The release of pent-up emotions and psychological tension through expression, resulting in emotional relief. Chi-Square Test A statistical test used to examine the association between two categorical variables. Chunking A memory strategy where information is grouped into larger, meaningful units, making it easier to recall. Classical Conditioning Learning where a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a meaningful one, eliciting a conditioned response (Pavlov). Client-Centred Therapy A humanistic approach by Carl Rogers emphasising unconditional positive regard, empathy and client autonomy. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) A widely used therapy focused on altering negative thought patterns and behaviours to treat psychological disorders. Cognitive Dissonance The discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or behaviours, motivating people to reduce the inconsistency (Festinger). Cognitive Distortions Irrational thought patterns (all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising) that lead to emotional distress (CBT framework). Cognitive Psychology The study of mental processes like memory, problem-solving, perception and decision-making. Conformity The tendency to change behaviour or beliefs to align with group norms, often under social pressure. D Defense Mechanisms Unconscious strategies that protect the ego — e.g. repression, displacement, projection (Freud). Degrees of Freedom (df) The number of values free to vary when calculating a statistic. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) An offshoot of CBT by Marsha Linehan, aimed at borderline personality disorder via mindfulness and emotion regulation. Displacement A defense mechanism where negative emotions are redirected from the original source to a less threatening target. Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21) A congenital condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to developmental and intellectual delays. E EEG (Electroencephalogram) A method for recording electrical activity in the brain using electrodes on the scalp. Extinction In classical conditioning, the weakening and disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is no longer paired with the US. Eclectic Therapy An approach combining elements from different therapeutic techniques to best meet the client's needs. Empiricism The belief that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience and observable evidence. Epigenetics The study of how environmental factors influence gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Ethnocentrism Viewing one's own culture as superior and judging other cultures by its standards. F Factor Analysis A statistical method to identify underlying relationships between variables, often used in psychometrics. Flashbulb Memory Vivid, detailed memories of significant, emotionally charged events, often resistant to decay. G Gate Control Theory A theory of pain perception: a neural "gate" in the spinal cord modulates pain by controlling signal flow to the brain. Gene A unit of heredity composed of DNA carrying genetic information that influences traits and characteristics. Genotype The genetic makeup of an individual, including dominant and recessive genes. Groupthink A phenomenon where group members prioritise consensus over critical thinking, leading to poor decisions. H Halo Effect A general impression of a person (positive or negative) influencing judgements about their other, unrelated traits. Hallucinations Sensory perceptions occurring without external stimuli, common in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. Hippocampus A brain structure crucial for forming new memories, particularly long-term memory processing. House-Tree-Person Test A projective test in which individuals draw a house, tree and person to assess personality traits. Hypothesis A testable prediction made by researchers, usually formed before an experiment. I Illusion A misperception or distortion of a sensory experience where perception does not match reality. Implicit Memory Memory that influences behaviour unconsciously, without intentional retrieval (e.g. procedural memory, riding a bike). Insight Learning A problem-solving process where understanding arises suddenly (Köhler's chimpanzee experiments). Insight-Oriented Therapy Psychotherapy aimed at helping clients gain awareness of unconscious thoughts, emotions and behaviours. Internal Locus of Control The belief that one controls one's own life events and outcomes, vs. external factors like luck or fate. J Just Noticeable Difference (JND) The smallest change in sensory stimulation a person can detect 50% of the time. Just-World Hypothesis A bias where people believe the world is fair, assuming individuals get what they deserve even in misfortune. K Klüver-Bucy Syndrome A disorder from temporal-lobe and amygdala damage, causing hypersexuality, visual agnosia and reduced fear responses. Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY) A genetic condition in males caused by an extra X chromosome, leading to developmental delays and specific physical traits. L Lateralisation of Brain Function Certain mental processes are specialised to the left or right hemisphere (e.g. language is typically left-hemisphere). Learned Helplessness Feeling unable to control or change a situation after repeated failure, leading to passivity and depression. Limbic System Brain structures regulating emotion, memory and motivation — includes hippocampus, amygdala and hypothalamus. Linguistic Relativity Hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf) Language influences thought and perception; speakers of different languages may experience the world differently. M Memory Systems The categorisation of memory into short-term, long-term and working memory, with subtypes like episodic and semantic. Null Hypothesis A statistical hypothesis stating there is no effect or difference; the baseline assumption in hypothesis testing. N Narcolepsy A sleep disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, often with muscle weakness (cataplexy). Neurotransmitters Chemical messengers across synapses — e.g. serotonin (mood), dopamine (reward), GABA (inhibitory). Neuroplasticity The brain's ability to reorganise and form new neural connections, especially after injury or during learning. Nomothetic Approach Seeking general laws that apply to all individuals (vs. the idiographic focus on the unique individual). Nurture Assumption The hypothesis that development is largely shaped by environment (nurture) rather than genetics (nature). O Object Permanence Understanding that objects continue to exist when unseen — Piaget's sensorimotor stage. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety. Operant Conditioning Skinner's theory of how behaviour is shaped by consequences, through reinforcement and punishment. Overgeneralisation A cognitive distortion: applying a single event or experience to an entire range of situations. P Phenotype The observable traits of an individual, influenced by both genetics and environment. Premack Principle In operant conditioning, high-probability behaviours reinforce low-probability ones ("games after homework"). Priming Exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a later stimulus, often outside conscious awareness. Projection A defense mechanism: attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts or motives to another person. Prosocial Behaviour Voluntary behaviour aimed at helping others, motivated by empathy or social norms. Psychoanalysis Freud's approach exploring unconscious thoughts and desires via free association and dream analysis. R Reinforcement In operant conditioning, increasing a behaviour by adding a positive outcome (positive) or removing an aversive stimulus (negative). Reciprocal Determinism Bandura's view that behaviour, environment and cognition all influence one another bidirectionally. Regression to the Mean Extreme data points tend to move closer to the average on subsequent measurements. Regression Analysis A statistical method to predict the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Reliability The consistency of a test or measure in producing stable, repeatable results (e.g. test-retest reliability). Retrograde Amnesia The inability to recall memories formed before the onset of amnesia. S Scaffolding In Vygotsky's theory, support from more knowledgeable others that helps a learner reach a higher level of understanding. Schemas Mental frameworks used to organise and interpret information, shaping perception and memory. Schizophrenia A severe disorder with hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech and impaired functioning. Short-Term Memory (STM) Temporary storage lasting ~15–30 seconds, with limited capacity. Social Learning Theory Bandura's view that learning occurs through observation, imitation and modelling, with reinforcement and punishment. Somatoform Disorders Disorders with physical symptoms lacking a medical cause — e.g. conversion disorder, hypochondriasis. Standardisation Establishing uniform procedures for administering and scoring tests to ensure consistency across situations. Stereotypes Oversimplified, generalised beliefs about groups of people, often based on race, gender or ethnicity. Stroop Test Naming the ink colour of a word, hardest when the word names a different colour (e.g. "red" printed in blue). T Temperament Biologically based tendencies to feel or act a certain way, present from early childhood; the foundation of personality. Transference In psychotherapy, clients projecting feelings and attitudes from past relationships onto the therapist. Transactional Analysis Eric Berne's theory examining interactions (transactions) based on Parent, Adult and Child ego states. T-Test A test comparing the means of two groups to see whether the difference is statistically significant. Turner Syndrome (XO) A condition in females from partial or complete absence of one X chromosome, with delayed development and infertility. U Unconditional Positive Regard Rogers' term for a therapist's non-judgemental acceptance and support of a client, regardless of what they say or do. Unconscious Motivation Desires, urges or thoughts that influence behaviour but exist outside conscious awareness (Freudian). Universal Emotions Per Paul Ekman, basic emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and fear are recognised and expressed similarly across all human cultures. V Validity The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to. Types: construct, criterion and content validity. Variable Ratio Schedule A reinforcement schedule rewarding behaviour after an unpredictable number of responses, giving high response rates (e.g. gambling). Visual Agnosia A disorder where a person can see but cannot recognise or interpret visual information, due to brain damage. W Working Memory Short-term memory that actively holds and manipulates information; crucial for reasoning, learning and comprehension. Wernicke's Area A region involved in language comprehension; damage causes Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech). X Xenophobia An irrational fear or dislike of people from other countries or cultures. X-Linked Disorders Genetic disorders from mutations on the X chromosome, often affecting males more severely (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia). Y Yerkes-Dodson Law Performance improves with arousal up to a point, after which further arousal hinders performance. Youth Bulge A demographic phenomenon where a large share of a population is young, often linked to social instability. Z Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) Vygotsky's gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance or collaboration. Zeigarnik Effect The tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones — tension aids memory. 4. 24 important therapies Founder · key concepts · techniques for each. NIMHANS/MET love "Therapy X was founded by?" and "Technique Y belongs to which therapy?" — drill both directions. Therapy Founder Key concepts Techniques 1. Animal-Assisted Therapy (AAT) No single founder (various psychologists & animal therapists) Uses animals (dogs, horses) to improve emotional well-being, enhance cognition and reduce stress; used for PTSD, anxiety, depression. Structured interaction with animals to build rapport and reduce anxiety. 2. Attachment Therapy Based on John Bowlby's attachment theory Building and repairing attachment bonds, often in children with trauma, neglect or inconsistent caregiving. Activities to build trust and strengthen the caregiver–child relationship. 3. Bibliotherapy No specific individual (used as an adjunct) Reading material that relates to the person's struggle to support healing and growth. Reading and discussing books, poetry or essays that give insight. 4. Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT) Anthony Ryle (1980s) Integrates cognitive and analytic approaches to understand problematic patterns of thinking, feeling and relating. Mapping behaviour patterns, identifying maladaptive thinking, reformulation letters to build insight. 5. Coherence Therapy Bruce Ecker & Laurel Hulley Symptoms arise from learned emotional responses; therapy uncovers and resolves them. Emotional uncovering, experiential work, creating moments of change. 6. Dance Movement Therapy (DMT) Marian Chace and other dance therapists (1940s) Movement as a form of expression to enhance emotional, cognitive and physical well-being. Movement exploration, body mirroring, expressive dance. 7. Developmental Needs Meeting Strategy (DNMS) Shirley Jean Schmidt Unmet childhood developmental needs drive adult emotional and psychological issues. Healing attachment wounds by meeting unmet developmental needs. 8. Dramatherapy Influenced by Jacob L. Moreno & Peter Slade Drama and theatre techniques to facilitate emotional expression, self-awareness and conflict resolution. Role-play, improvisation, storytelling, guided imagery. 9. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation & Reprocessing) Francine Shapiro (1987) Treats trauma by processing distressing memories and reducing their impact; client recalls trauma while focusing on bilateral stimuli. Eye movements, bilateral tapping, cognitive restructuring of traumatic memories. 10. Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP) Robert Kohlenberg & Mavis Tsai Uses the therapeutic relationship to change problematic interpersonal behaviours as they emerge in session. Reinforcing adaptive behaviour in the relationship, in-vivo exposure, emotional validation. 11. Hypnotherapy Modern form attributed to Milton Erickson (roots in Franz Mesmer, 18th c.) Hypnosis to create focused attention, heightened suggestibility and deep relaxation; used for phobias, addictions, chronic pain. Trance induction, suggestion therapy. 12. Integral Therapy Ken Wilber Integral theory integrating multiple perspectives — internal/external, individual/collective — into a holistic whole. Working across four quadrants to create a holistic approach to therapy and development. 13. Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) Habib Davanloo Active therapy to overcome resistance and access repressed emotions; tackles deep-rooted problems in a short time. Emotionally focused interventions, unlocking the unconscious, working through defenses. 14. Logotherapy Viktor Frankl Existential therapy centred on finding meaning in life, even amid suffering; humans are driven by a "will to meaning." Socratic dialogue, dereflection, paradoxical intention. 15. Metacognitive Therapy Adrian Wells Modifies dysfunctional metacognitive beliefs that maintain anxiety and depression. Detachment from thought processes, attention training, challenging metacognitive beliefs. 16. Multimodal Therapy (MMT) Arnold Lazarus Evaluates seven dimensions of personality — the BASIC ID: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs/biology. Tailored interventions for each modality based on the person's specific needs. 17. Narrative Therapy Michael White & David Epston Sees people as separate from their problems; clients "re-author" their lives with empowering narratives. Externalising problems, identifying unique outcomes, re-authoring personal stories. 18. Play Therapy Virginia Axline & Carl Rogers (influences) Play as a medium for children to express emotions, resolve conflicts and process difficult experiences. Sand tray, role-playing, art-based activities, storytelling. 19. Positive Psychotherapy Nossrat Peseschkian Emphasises inherent capacities for growth and healing; focuses on strengths rather than pathology. Balancing techniques, active goal-setting, identifying personal strengths. 20. Rational Living Therapy (RLT) Aldo R. Pucci A cognitive-behavioural approach building on REBT to replace irrational beliefs with more logical ones. Cognitive restructuring, disputing irrational beliefs, a rational-living plan. 21. Reality Therapy William Glasser Based on choice theory: clients take control of their lives by making better choices; emphasises personal responsibility and the present. Action planning, focusing on current behaviour, exploring new choices. 22. Sexual Identity Therapy No single founder Addresses sexual orientation, identity and gender identity in a supportive, affirming way. Exploratory discussion, psychoeducation, supportive counselling. 23. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg Short-term, goal-oriented; finds solutions in the present rather than dwelling on past problems. Miracle question, scaling questions, identifying exceptions. 24. Structural Family Therapy Salvador Minuchin Looks at family hierarchies, boundaries and subsystems and how they shape individual behaviour and mental health. Joining, restructuring family interactions, boundary setting. 5. 25 landmark experiments The classic studies, with who ran them, when, where and what they showed. The entrances ask these as "Experiment X was conducted by?" and "Which study demonstrated effect Y?". Experiment Conducted by Year Where What it showed 1. Hawthorne Studies Elton Mayo 1924–1932 Western Electric, Hawthorne Works, Chicago Productivity rose when workers knew they were observed — the Hawthorne effect . 2. Little Albert Experiment John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 1920 Johns Hopkins University A baby was classically conditioned to fear a white rat; fear generalised to similar stimuli. Now a landmark in research ethics. 3. Halo Effect Experiment Edward Thorndike 1920 Case Western University A positive impression of one quality (e.g. attractiveness) led people to overestimate other qualities. 4. The Monster Study Wendell Johnson 1939 University of Iowa Attempted to induce stuttering in orphan children through negative speech therapy — one of the most unethical studies in psychology. 5. Robbers Cave Experiment Muzafer Sherif 1954 Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma Intergroup conflict arises between groups and is resolved through superordinate goals . 6. Asch Conformity Experiment Solomon Asch 1951 Swarthmore College Participants conformed to clearly wrong answers given by a group — the power of social pressure. 7. Cognitive Dissonance Experiment Leon Festinger 1957 Stanford University Discomfort when behaviour conflicts with belief; participants justified their behaviour by changing their beliefs. 8. Harlow's Monkey Experiment Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Infant monkeys preferred a cloth "mother" (comfort) over a wire one (food) — contact comfort drives attachment. 9. Fantz Looking Chamber Experiment Robert Fantz 1961 Case Western Reserve University Infants preferred looking at human faces over patterns — innate visual preferences. 10. Bobo Doll Experiment Albert Bandura 1961 Stanford University Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll imitated it — observational / social learning. 11. Milgram Obedience Experiment Stanley Milgram 1961 Yale University Participants administered what they believed were painful shocks when told to by an authority — obedience over morality. 12. Schachter & Singer Experiment on Emotion Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer 1962 Columbia University Supported the two-factor theory of emotion (arousal + cognitive labelling); participants misattributed arousal based on others' behaviour. 13. Ainsworth Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth 1969 Johns Hopkins University Assessed infant attachment via reaction to a caregiver's absence/return; three styles — secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant. 14. Split-Brain Experiment Roger Sperry 1968 California Institute of Technology Studied severed-corpus-callosum patients; showed the two hemispheres have specialised functions (Nobel Prize). 15. The Good Samaritan Experiment John Darley & C. Daniel Batson 1973 Princeton University Situational factors (being in a hurry) drove helping more than values — even among theology students. 16. Stanford Prison Experiment Philip Zimbardo 1971 Stanford University A simulated prison showed the extreme psychological effects of perceived power; guards turned abusive, prisoners traumatised — ended early. 17. Marshmallow Test Walter Mischel 1972 Stanford University A longitudinal study of delayed gratification in children; those who waited for a larger reward had better later outcomes. 18. Bystander Effect (Good Samaritan study) John Darley & Bibb Latané 1968 Columbia University People are less likely to help in distress when others are present — responsibility is diffused. 19. Ross's False Consensus Effect Study Lee Ross 1977 Stanford University People overestimate how much others share their beliefs, attitudes and behaviours — the false consensus effect . 20. Selective Attention (The Invisible Gorilla) Daniel Simons & Christopher Chabris 1999 Harvard University Counting basketball passes, many viewers missed a gorilla walking through — inattentional blindness . 21. Car Crash Experiment Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer 1974 University of California, Irvine The misinformation effect : question wording ("smashed" vs "hit") altered recalled speed of the cars. 22. A Class Divided Jane Elliott 1968 Riceville, Iowa After MLK's assassination, Elliott split her class by eye colour, treating one group as superior then reversing it — showing prejudice is arbitrary and damaging. 23. Learned Helplessness Experiment Martin Seligman 1967 University of Pennsylvania Dogs given unavoidable shocks stopped trying to escape even when they could — learned helplessness , a model for depression. 24. Surrogate Mother Experiment (Harlow's monkeys) Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Monkeys offered a wire mother (food) and a cloth mother (comfort) chose comfort — contact comfort over feeding. 25. Visual Cliff Experiment Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk 1960 Cornell University Infants placed on a glass surface over an apparent drop avoided the "cliff" — depth perception develops early.

title: Biopsychology & Neuroscience
text: Biopsychology & Neuroscience The biology of behaviour from first principles: how neurons fire and talk, how the nervous system is built and mapped, the transmitter systems and their drugs, and the circuits behind sensation, movement, memory, hunger, hormones, sleep, stress, emotion, addiction and psychiatric disorders, anchored to Pinel & Barnes and deepened with Carlson, prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. In this book Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics & experience Anatomy of the nervous system The cranial nerves (I–XII) Neural conduction & the action potential Synaptic transmission & neurotransmitter systems Research methods of biopsychology The visual system Audition & the other senses The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage & neuroplasticity Learning, memory & amnesia Hunger, eating & health Hormones, sex & the HPA axis Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms Reward, drugs of abuse & addiction Lateralisation, language & the split brain Emotion, stress & health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & batteries Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Landmark studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience The one idea behind the whole field. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is the branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system) that keeps behaviour at the centre. The recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue. The six divisions of biopsychology The field is split by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study Trap Psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients. Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is the field's signature methodological value. Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony: prefer the simplest explanation that fits; do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. High-yield Human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Causation needs a true experiment; trust the conclusion many methods agree on. 2. Evolution, genetics & experience The problem this fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability). Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses. Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. Humans have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Approaches to human cognition Eysenck & Keane open by saying cognitive psychology is not one method but four converging approaches , each with its own logic and limits. The point of knowing all four is that an exam stem will describe a technique and ask which approach it belongs to. Experimental cognitive psychology What it claims: you can infer the hidden stages of mental processing in healthy people by measuring behaviour under controlled conditions — chiefly reaction time (RT) and accuracy/error rate . It is the oldest strand and the historical core of the field. If a manipulation slows people down, that stage must require processing. Key logic: the subtraction/additive-factors idea — compare two tasks differing in one operation, and the RT difference estimates that operation's duration. Limit: behaviour alone is ambiguous about the underlying architecture (many models predict the same RT), and lab tasks may lack ecological validity. Cognitive neuropsychology + modularity What it claims: studying brain-damaged patients reveals the normal architecture of cognition, because damage can knock out one ability while sparing another. The bedrock assumption is modularity (Fodor): the mind contains specialised, domain-specific, informationally encapsulated modules that can be independently impaired. Key logic — the double dissociation : patient A is impaired on task X but fine on Y, while patient B is fine on X but impaired on Y. That pattern is strong evidence the two tasks rely on separate systems (one alone could be explained by task difficulty). Example: H.M. lost the ability to form new long-term memories yet had normal short-term span; other patients (e.g. K.F.) show the reverse — together a double dissociation of STM and LTM. Limit: damage is rarely clean, the brain reorganises, and single cases generalise poorly. Cognitive neuroscience methods What it claims: by measuring the living brain we can locate where and time when cognition happens. The methods trade off spatial against temporal resolution, and the exam loves to ask which method gives which. Method Measures Strength fMRI Blood-oxygen (BOLD) — indirect metabolic signal Excellent spatial resolution (mm), poor temporal (seconds); shows where . PET Radioactive tracer, blood flow/metabolism Good spatial, very poor temporal; needs injected tracer. EEG / ERP Scalp electrical activity; ERP = signal averaged to an event Excellent temporal resolution (ms), poor spatial; shows when . TMS Magnetic pulse that briefly disrupts a region Creates a "virtual lesion" → tests if a region is necessary (causal, not just correlational). Spatial vs temporal mnemonic: fMRI/PET = WHERE (great space, poor time). EEG/ERP = WHEN (great time, poor space). TMS = whether it's NECESSARY (causal). fMRI and EEG are merely correlational; only TMS and lesions establish that a region is causally required. Computational cognitive science & connectionism (PDP) What it claims: if a theory is precise enough, you can implement it as a running computer program; a model that actually reproduces human performance (including human errors ) is a strong test of the theory. The dominant style is connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) : networks of simple, neuron-like units connected by weighted links, where knowledge is distributed across the pattern of weights rather than stored in one location, and learning happens by gradually adjusting weights (e.g. back-propagation). NIMHANS tests harder — connectionism. Be ready for the contrast with classical "symbolic" models. Symbolic (e.g. Newell & Simon's physical-symbol-system) manipulates discrete rules and symbols, processing serially. Connectionist/PDP uses distributed sub-symbolic representations and parallel processing; its hallmarks are graceful degradation (partial damage = partial loss, not total crash), generalisation, and learning from examples. NIMHANS may ask which framework explains prototype effects or developmental error patterns (e.g. the U-shaped curve in learning the past tense) — that's connectionism. Top-down (concept-driven) processing brings expectations, context and stored knowledge to bear. Assimilation — fitting new info into an existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying the schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Animism — preoperational; attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time; blocks conservation. The Ahuja page reads the field as Indian psychiatry: definitions, criteria, drugs, fast and exam-tight. Barlow & Durand reads it as integrative science : it refuses any single cause and forces every disorder through a multidimensional model , and it teaches from cases . That's the angle this page adds. Use Ahuja for the cut-offs and drugs, use this for the model questions ("which approach / what causes it / which dimension"). Two ideas hold the whole book together. (1) The multidimensional integrative model. No disorder has one cause; each is the product of biological (genes, brain circuits, neurotransmitters), psychological (learning, cognition, conditioning), emotional , social/cultural and developmental dimensions interacting. (2) Diathesis-stress run forward in time. A vulnerability (diathesis) only becomes a disorder when life delivers the stress; genes and environment are not separate but reciprocal (your genes shape the environments you pick), and experience switches genes on and off ( epigenetics ). What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions Barlow & Durand do not use a "4 Ds" list. Their working definition of a psychological disorder has three components , and all three usually travel together: (1) psychological dysfunction — a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; (2) distress or impairment — it hurts the person or wrecks their day-to-day functioning; (3) an atypical or culturally unexpected response — it deviates from what the culture expects (and is not merely a deviant act society dislikes). They lean on Wakefield's "harmful dysfunction" : a disorder is a failure of an internal mechanism to do what it evolved to do ( dysfunction ) and that failure is harmful to the person by their culture's standards. B&D's 3 vs Ahuja's 4 Ds. If a question cites " dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected ," that's the Barlow & Durand definition (3 components). The "Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger" 4-D list is the more common Indian-text framing. Danger is NOT one of B&D's three. Both agree dysfunction/impairment is the indispensable core and distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient (a person in mania feels great). The book ends every chapter by scoring the theorist on six recurring Questions About Human Nature . Hold these six and you can predict any theorist's "view of the person" answer: (1) free will vs determinism · (2) nature vs nurture (heredity vs environment) · (3) past vs present (does childhood fix us, or does the here-and-now/future drive us) · (4) uniqueness vs universality · (5) equilibrium vs growth (is the basic motive to reduce tension and stay balanced, or to grow ) · (6) optimism vs pessimism . Freud is the dark end of all six; the humanists are the bright end. Everyone else sits between. Part One · The study of personality Ch 1. Personality: what it is, and how the book studies it Personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that characterises a person and how they adapt to the world. The word comes from the Latin persona , the mask the Roman actor wore, which already hides the book's central tension: is personality the mask we show, or the real face behind it? Every theory in the book is one answer to four questions: what is personality made of , where does it come from , why do people differ , and can it change . The book groups the theorists into approaches , and that grouping is the spine of the table of contents: the psychoanalytic (Freud); the neopsychoanalytic (Jung, Adler, Horney); the life-span (Erikson); the genetics/trait pioneer (Allport); the humanistic (Maslow, Rogers); the cognitive (Kelly); the behavioural (Skinner); the social-learning (Bandura); the trait approach (Cattell, Eysenck, the Five-Factor Model); and the facet / limited-domain theories (Rotter, Zuckerman, Seligman). How the book assesses and researches personality The book insists every theory must answer two practical questions, and the recurring "Assessment" and "Research" sections grade each theorist on them: Assessment = how do you measure this theory's constructs? The methods recur: self-report inventories (objective, scored against norms, e.g. MMPI, 16PF, NEO), projective techniques (ambiguous stimuli, e.g. Rorschach, TAT), clinical interviews , behavioural assessment , and idiographic personal documents (diaries, letters). A good test must clear three bars: reliability (consistency), validity (measures what it claims), and standardised norms . Research = how was the theory tested ? Three designs recur: the clinical method (case studies, the dominant psychoanalytic tool, rich but unreliable and unrepresentative), the experimental method (manipulate a variable, the only route to cause and effect), and the correlational method (relate two measured variables, covariation only, never causation). TRAP — method by camp. Case study / clinical method = the psychoanalysts (Freud, Jung, Adler). Correlational + factor analysis = the trait theorists (Cattell, Eysenck, FFM). Controlled experiment = the behaviourists and social-learning theorists (Skinner, Bandura) and Rogers, who pioneered experimental psychotherapy research. The method usually tells you the camp. Recap Ch 1. Personality = the enduring, distinctive pattern of how a person thinks, feels and behaves. The book is organised by approach and grades every theorist on six human-nature issues plus Assessment and Research. Nomothetic (general laws, trait research) vs idiographic (the unique individual, case studies) is the master methodological split. Part Two · The psychoanalytic approach Ch 2. Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives What the field claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it settles questions by study, not intuition. The governing insight, repeated throughout, is the power of the situation : ordinary people help, conform, obey and aggress far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Milgram), bystander apathy (Latané & Darley) and attribution (the fundamental attribution error is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good science runs a loop: a theory generates a falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute it. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed. The core research methods Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold all else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. Systematic / naturalistic observation Watch and record behaviour as it occurs without intervening (e.g. counting jaywalkers). High realism. Limit: no control, observer effects, no causal claim. High-yield The IV is the cause you dial (the knob), the DV the effect you read off (the dial). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not pre-existing differences between people, moved the dial; correlational work has no knob, so it cannot tell you which dial drives. A mediator is the mechanism between cause and effect, explaining why (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship, telling you when / for whom it holds (heat raises aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true effect size. Ethics, deception and replication Because the true purpose can change behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story), permitted only under strict safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing that reveals the true purpose and removes any after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The field also takes its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classics (Milgram, marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. The four perspectives Baron uses Perspective Core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution live here). Evolutionary Some tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection for survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain and biology (fMRI, hormones): amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many findings hold differently across cultures; must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). High-yield The researcher is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist partly to fence out the researcher's expectancy bias / experimenter effects.
