title: Psychological Assessment & Testing
text: Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it must be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability . Accurate = validity . Everything in this chapter is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or a real-world test built on those foundations. We measure things we cannot see directly (anxiety, intelligence, personality) by building instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions, then deciding things with them: special education, army fitness, diagnosis. This chapter locks the psychometric theory first, then the major intelligence, personality, projective, and clinical instruments, with every author, year, item count, scale, score range, and exam trap in one place. In this book Item analysis & test construction Reliability (the consistency story) Validity (the accuracy story) Norms & standard scores Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics Stanford-Binet family Wechsler family Raven’s Progressive Matrices Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Group & infant/developmental scales Indian intelligence tests IQ classification & intellectual disability Objective (self-report) personality tests Projective tests Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Educational measurement basics Master reference tables & trap list 1. Item analysis & test construction Each test item is a single sensor reading. If a sensor is too easy (everyone passes) it tells us nothing; too hard (no one passes) it tells us nothing; and if it disagrees with the rest of the test, something is wrong with it. That is why every well-built test goes through item analysis. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is the proportion who got an item right. p = (number correct) / (total attempting) , range 0 to 1. p = 0.50 is the sweet spot for a free-response item because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ the optimal p is ~0.625 , halfway between chance guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). p above 0.80 = too easy; p below 0.20 = too hard. Both are revision candidates because they cannot separate strong from weak students. Discrimination index, D Do high-scorers on the whole test do better on this item than low-scorers? D = p_upper − p_lower , where p_upper = proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower = proportion in the bottom 27%. Range −1 to +1. D above 0.40 = item agrees with the test, a good signal. D near zero = random noise; both groups perform alike. Negative D = the bottom group out-performed the top group: the item is mis-keyed, ambiguous, or has a trick strong test-takers over-think. Trap Read negative discrimination as a mis-keyed / flawed item to discard immediately , NOT as a merely “hard” item. This is asked every cycle. 2. Reliability (the consistency story) Reliability is not about whether a test is correct; it is about whether it is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time is reliable even if your true weight is 70 (that is a validity problem). A scale bouncing between 60, 90, 80 is unreliable, full stop. If a test is unreliable you cannot trust any single score: the same person retested gives a different answer for reasons unrelated to the trait. You are measuring noise. Definition Classical Test Theory: Observed Score = True Score + Error . Reliability is the proportion of observed-score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% signal, 20% noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice (test-retest). Across forms: give two equivalent versions (parallel/alternate forms). Within one administration, across items: check items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest (time stability) Give the test, give it again later, correlate the two scores. High correlation = stable over time. The standard window is two to four weeks . Too long and the trait itself can change (correlation drops, but the test is not at fault); too short and memory carryover inflates the correlation. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split into two halves (often odd vs even items), correlate the halves. By splitting you have halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable, so the raw split-half correlation under estimates full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects this: r_full = 2 × r_half / (1 + r_half) . Example: r_half = 0.60 → r_full = 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75 . Always apply Spearman-Brown after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half and averaging the result: that mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point (e.g. Likert) items. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and trait variance. Trap Alpha is NOT a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still measure two distinct constructs. The MET loves this. KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20) When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1/0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to KR-20: same idea, adapted for 0/1 items. So “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?” → KR-20 . Inter-rater: kappa and ICC When humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades), reliability is about rater agreement. Cohen kappa for categorical decisions (OCD: yes/no), corrects for chance agreement. Kappa ≥ 0.81 = almost-perfect; 0.61–0.80 = substantial. Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous ratings (a 0–100 severity score); different ICC forms exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Trap Kappa is NOT an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure tes

title: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics
text: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics One consolidated chapter for everything the MET / NIMHANS paper tests on treatment: the learning principles that behaviour therapy is built on, the major schools of psychotherapy & counselling (Sharf's frame, school by school, with the third-wave and integrative models folded in), the common therapeutic factors that cut across schools, and professional ethics . Each concept lives in exactly one place. The exam tests four moves: name the theory from its claim; pin the theory to its founder; pin the named technique to its theory; and tell rival theories apart, because that is where the distractor always hides. Learn every technique in its contrast pair . In this book Learning & conditioning: the foundation How to read any theory (the master frame) Psychodynamic approaches Humanistic & existential approaches Behavioural & cognitive approaches Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches Third-wave, integrative & specialised models Group therapy (Yalom) Common factors & the therapeutic frame Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Professional ethics Master trap list, rosters & glossary High-yield The single most-tested skill is telling near-identical pairs apart: REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Beck) , systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding , ERP (OCD) vs EMDR (trauma) , cognitive triad (Beck) vs ABC (Ellis) , DBT modules (4) vs ACT hexaflex (6) , and the four family-therapy founders (Bowen / Minuchin / Haley / Satir). And in learning: shaping vs chaining , fading vs extinction , VR vs VI , latent vs insight learning . Master these pairs and most of the section answers itself. 1. Learning & conditioning: the foundation of behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy is applied learning theory, so the vocabulary below is tested both as 1-mark definition traps and as the mechanism behind clinical techniques. Read this orientation once: classical (Pavlovian) conditioning is about stimulus pairings ; operant (Skinnerian) conditioning is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour ; priming is about one stimulus making a later one easier to process ; and habituation / sensitization are non-associative (a single stimulus, no pairing). When a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant reinforcement schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Tolman), insight learning (Köhler), observational learning (Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) 1.1 Operant shaping tools — shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Shaping (Skinner): reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism does not yet emit . Train a rat to press a lever by reinforcing facing it, then approaching, then touching, then pressing. The defining feature is that the reinforcement criterion changes across trials . Clinically: skill acquisition, autism intervention. Chaining : linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour is the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next and only the final link is reinforced (brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet → paste → brush → rinse → put away). Forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first, so the learner always reaches the reinforcer at the natural endpoint (often preferred clinically). Used heavily in ABA / ADL skills training. Prompting : an added antecedent stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the right response in the presence of the natural cue. Prompt hierarchy, most → least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are classic vignette distractors. Fading : gradually removing the prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue (teach "ball": full model "say ball" → partial "say buh…" → just holding up the ball). Trap Shaping vs chaining: shaping builds a new behaviour ; chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs extinction: fading removes the prompt (an antecedent) and transfers stimulus control; extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS and eliminates the behaviour. Prompts are antecedents; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested directly. 1.2 Classical conditioning phenomena Extinction : reduction and disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented — Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the unpaired bell; the ignored tantrum fades. Watch for the extinction burst : a temporary increase in frequency/intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before decline. Extinction does not erase learning. Spontaneous recovery : reappearance of a previously extinguished response after a rest period, with no new conditioning trials — proving extinction is suppression, not unlearning . The recovered response is typically weaker , and re-extinction is faster the second time (savings effect). Distinguish from reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) and renewal (re-emergence in a new context). Generalization vs discrimination. Generalization = responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D (Little Albert, conditioned by Watson & Rayner to fear a white rat, also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard). The generalization gradient : response strength drops with distance from the original CS. Discrimination = responding only to the specific stimulus, taught by differential reinforcement (reinforce in presence of S D , withhold for S Δ ). One-liner: generalization is the default; discrimination is trained. Failure to discriminate underlies many phobias. Note: stimul

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics One consolidated, exam-ready treatment built from A. K. Singh ( Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences — strong on measurement, test construction, item analysis) and Coolican ( Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology — design, the logic of inference, which test to run). Read the prose and understand why each statistic does what it does; the tables are then just reminders. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built on. Coverage runs MET 2026 depth with NIMHANS M.Phil clinical extensions where the entrance pushes harder. In this book Research design & methodology Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Validity & threats in a study Sampling Levels of measurement Reliability & validity in measurement Scaling (attitude measurement) Item analysis & test construction Descriptive statistics Distributions, z-scores & the Central Limit Theorem The logic of inference Parametric tests Non-parametric tests Correlation, regression & special coefficients Degrees of freedom — from scratch Qualitative & mixed methods Clinical trials & reporting standards Research ethics Decision table: which test do I use? Collected MCQ traps Worked intuition Fast glossary Research design & methodology Only an experiment (manipulate the IV and randomly assign participants) can establish causation, because randomisation balances out unknown confounds. Everything else can describe and relate, but not prove cause. Experimental hierarchy — by degree of control Design Manipulate IV? Random assignment? Control group? Internal validity True experimental (RCT) Yes Yes Yes High — gold standard for causation Quasi-experimental Yes No (intact/pre-existing groups: classes, wards) Usually yes Moderate — confounds remain Pre-experimental Loosely No Often none Low — e.g. one-group pretest-posttest; many threats Non-experimental (correlational) No — — No causal claim Between- vs within-subjects (and factorial) Between-subjects (independent groups): different people in each condition. No carry-over, but between-person variability is noise and groups may differ to start. Within-subjects (repeated measures): the same people in every condition. Each is their own control, so it is powerful and economical, but risks order/carry-over effects (practice, fatigue) — fixed by counterbalancing . Factorial: two or more IVs crossed, so you can test their interaction (a 2×2 has 4 cells). Specific designs to know Pretest-posttest control group: the classic two-group RCT. Posttest-only control group: avoids pretest sensitisation entirely. Solomon four-group: combines both. Two groups get a pretest, two do not; half of each get treatment. It detects and separates pretest sensitisation (the interaction of pretest and treatment) from the treatment effect itself. Resource-heavy but the most rigorous design for ruling out testing effects. Crossover design: every subject receives both conditions in different order. Single-case designs (ABA, ABAB, multiple baseline): used in behaviour analysis. Non-experimental & epidemiological designs Correlational: measure variables as they are and relate them; no manipulation, so no causal claim. Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; reports prevalence . Cheap, but cannot show temporality or change. Longitudinal: the same people followed over time; can show change and causal order, but slow, costly, and bleeds participants through attrition . Cohort study: follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time; reports relative risk . Case-control: start with cases and controls, look back at exposure; reports odds ratio . Case study: deep dive into one person/unit (rich, hypothesis-generating, not generalisable). Observational: watch behaviour in situ — naturalistic vs structured; participant vs non-participant; covert vs overt. Controlling confounds Randomisation — random assignment spreads unknown confounds evenly across groups (the most powerful control). Counterbalancing — vary the order of conditions across subjects to cancel order effects in within-subjects designs. Matching — pair subjects on a key variable (e.g. IQ) before assigning, removing that variable as a confound. Single-blind (participant unaware of condition) and double-blind (participant and experimenter/assessor unaware) — control expectancy and experimenter effects. Trap Random sampling vs random assignment . Random sampling = who gets into the study (drives external validity/generalisability). Random assignment = which condition they go to (drives internal validity/causation). A study can have one without the other. Trap Counterbalancing (fixes order effects in within-subjects designs) vs matching (controls a specific confound variable in between-subjects designs). Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Independent variable (IV): what the experimenter manipulates or groups by — the presumed cause. Dependent variable (DV): the measured outcome — the presumed effect. Control variable: a variable deliberately held constant. Confound: a variable tied to both the IV and the DV, creating a spurious link and offering a rival explanation. Controlled by randomisation, matching, or statistical adjustment. Extraneous variable: any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; it becomes a confound only if it also correlates with the IV. Operationalisation: defining a fuzzy construct in concrete, measurable terms (e.g. "anxiety" = score on the GAD-7). Bad operationalisation sinks construct validity. Mediator vs moderator — the high-frequency trap Both are "third variables," but they do opposite jobs: Mediator explains HOW / WHY the IV affects the DV — the mechanism in the causal chain: IV → Mediator → DV . Stress → cortisol → poorer immunity: cortisol mediates. If you control the mediator, the IV–DV link weakens or vanishes. Tested with Baron-Kenny steps or Hayes PROCESS. Moderator changes WHEN / FOR WHOM / HOW STRONGLY the IV affects the DV — it alters the strength or directio

title: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction
text: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction The science of measuring the mind: how a psychological test is built, scored and judged. This book teaches the four scales of measurement, the anatomy of a good item and how to analyse one, the full reliability and validity families with their formulae, the meaning of norms and standard scores, and the major families of real tests – intelligence, neuropsychological, personality, interest and aptitude – together with where and why each is applied (education, occupation, military, clinic). It closes with the M.Phil-style exam questions folded in. Sourced from Rodrick Prashanth's Unit 3 decks (Areas of testing, Applications of testing, Interest & aptitude tests, Item writing & item analysis, Reliability/Validity/Norms, Scales) and the M.Phil question bank, deepened to NIMHANS clinical depth. In this book Scales of measurement & attitude scaling Item writing & item analysis Reliability Validity Norms & standard scores Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment Areas of testing: personality assessment Interest & aptitude tests Applications of testing Structured personality-test construction M.Phil exam questions 1. Scales of measurement & attitude scaling The one idea. Before you can measure a psychological attribute you must decide what kind of number you are assigning. S. S. Stevens' four levels of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio – form a ladder: each rung adds one mathematical property and therefore unlocks one more legitimate statistic. Choosing the wrong scale is the commonest hidden error in test interpretation: you cannot average ranks, and you cannot say one IQ is "twice" another. The four levels Level Allows categorising Allows ranking (order) Equal intervals True (absolute) zero Example Nominal Yes – – – Diagnosis codes, gender, jersey numbers Ordinal Yes Yes – – Rank in class, Likert agree/disagree, race finishing order Interval Yes Yes Yes – Temperature in °C, IQ scores, calendar years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Yes Reaction time, weight, number of errors, age Why each property matters. A nominal scale only labels – the numbers are names, so the only legitimate operations are counting frequencies and the mode. An ordinal scale adds order, so you can take a median and percentiles, but the gaps between ranks are unequal (the difference between 1st and 2nd is not the same "amount" as between 2nd and 3rd). An interval scale adds equal spacing, so you can finally add, subtract and compute a mean and standard deviation; but its zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"). A ratio scale adds a true zero meaning total absence of the attribute, so ratios become meaningful: 40 errors is genuinely twice 20 errors. High-yield Memorise the ladder of properties: N ominal = categorise; O rdinal = + order; I nterval = + equal intervals; R atio = + true zero. Each level permits everything the levels below it permit, plus one more. Mnemonic NOIR (French for "black") gives the order of increasing power: N ominal → O rdinal → I nterval → R atio. Trap Interval vs ratio. Both have equal intervals; only ratio has a true zero. IQ and Celsius temperature are interval – an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence," so you cannot say IQ 140 is "twice as smart" as IQ 70. Kelvin temperature and reaction time are ratio. Attitude scales Attitude measurement applies these principles to subjective opinion. The deck names four classic formats: Scale Structure Key feature Likert scale Five ordered responses on an agree/disagree or approve/disapprove continuum (e.g. Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree) Summative; the most widely used attitude format. Strictly ordinal, though usually treated as interval in practice. Guttman scale Items ordered by intensity; a respondent who endorses one statement also endorses all milder statements on the same continuum Cumulative / unidimensional. "Check the statement from each group that is most true of you." Semantic differential (Osgood) A set of bipolar adjective scales (Healthy – Unhealthy, Pleasant – Unpleasant) anchoring a 7-point line Measures the subjective meaning and affective reaction to a concept; classic dimensions are Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Stapel scale A single ( unipolar ) adjective with 10 categories from −5 to +5, no neutral zero A one-adjective alternative to the semantic differential; forces a direction. Trap Semantic differential vs Stapel. Semantic differential uses bipolar adjective pairs with a neutral midpoint; the Stapel scale uses a single (unipolar) adjective on a −5 to +5 line with no neutral point . Guttman is cumulative (endorsing a strong item implies endorsing the weaker ones); Likert is summative. 2. Item writing & item analysis The one idea. A test is only as good as its items. Item construction is part craft (writing clear, unambiguous questions) and part statistics (keeping the items that actually discriminate among people and dropping those that do not). Item analysis is the set of empirical methods for that pruning. Guidelines for item writing (DeVellis, 2012) Define clearly what you want to measure before writing anything. Generate an item pool larger than the final test, so weak items can be discarded. Avoid exceptionally long items – length adds reading load, not information. Keep reading difficulty appropriate to the intended respondents. Avoid "double-barrelled" items that pack two ideas into one statement ("I feel anxious and depressed") – the respondent cannot answer cleanly. Mix positively and negatively worded items to counter acquiescence (yea-saying) response bias. Item formats & correction for guessing The dichotomous format scores an item 0 or 1 (true/false, right/wrong). The polytomous format gives each item more than two alternatives. In a multiple-choice item, the incorrect alternatives are called distractors ; it is usually best to write three or four good distractors per item, and three distractors are about as effectiv

title: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour The full biological machinery of behaviour, built from the ground up: how a single neuron is wired and how it fires, the chemical languages it speaks, how those neurons are assembled into the brain and the rest of the nervous system, and the circuits that drive movement, every sense, hunger and thirst, emotion, the hormones and glands, sleep, heredity, and the methods scientists use to take the whole system apart. Anchored to Carlson & Pinel-level neuroscience and prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology. In this book Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse Neurotransmitters Structure & functions of the nervous system Divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS, ANS) Divisions of the human brain & their functions The motor (sensorimotor) system Sensory systems — vision Auditory & somatosensory systems Chemical & vestibular senses Hunger & thirst Emotions Hormonal regulation of behaviour The glandular (endocrine) system Sleep & biological clocks Genetics & behaviour Invasive & non-invasive research methods 1. Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse The neuron is the information-processing and information-transmitting element of the nervous system. Everything else in this unit is about how neurons are built, how they fire, how they talk to each other, and how billions of them are wired into the brain. Master the neuron first and the rest of the unit becomes mechanism rather than memorisation. The four regions of a neuron Part What it is Function Cell body (soma) Contains the nucleus and most of the cell's life-support machinery; shape varies widely between neuron types. Keeps the cell alive; integrates incoming signals. Dendrites Branching projections; the major receivers of messages. Receive neural messages transmitted across the synapse (the small gap between a terminal button and the dendrite). Axon A long slender tube, often myelinated; works like an electrical cord. Carries the action potential away from the soma toward the terminal buttons. Terminal buttons Little knobs at the ends of axon branches. When an action potential arrives, they secrete a chemical messenger, the neurotransmitter . Definition Action potential — a brief electrical event that starts at the axon end nearest the cell body (the axon initial segment) and travels toward the terminal buttons. It is the basic message the axon carries. Axoplasmic transport Terminal buttons need molecules that can only be made in the soma, so substances are moved along the axon along microtubule "tracks". This is an active process, separate from the action potential. Anterograde transport (soma → terminal): accomplished by the motor protein kinesin , which "walks" along microtubules carrying cargo. Remarkably fast, up to 500 mm/day. Retrograde transport (terminal → soma): accomplished by the protein dynein ; about half as fast as anterograde transport. Types (classes) of neurons Multipolar neuron — more than two processes extending from the cell body (the most common type). Unipolar neuron — one process extending from the cell body (e.g. sensory dorsal-root neurons). Bipolar neuron — two processes (e.g. in the retina). Interneurons — neurons with a short axon or no axon at all; they integrate neural activity within a single brain structure . Neuroanatomical gross structures Composed of In the CNS In the PNS Mostly cell bodies Nuclei Ganglia Mostly axons Tracts Nerves Trap Cell-body clusters are nuclei in the CNS but ganglia in the PNS; axon bundles are tracts in the CNS but nerves in the PNS. The paper loves to swap these. Glial cells There are roughly equal numbers of neurons and glia in the human brain. Four kinds matter: Oligodendrocytes — paddle-shaped processes that wrap myelin around axons in the CNS . A single oligodendrocyte produces up to 50 segments of myelin. Myelin is 80% lipid, 20% protein and speeds axonal conduction. Schwann cells — perform myelination in the PNS ; one Schwann cell wraps one axon entirely. After PNS injury they digest dead axons and form cylinders that guide axonal regrowth, which is why PNS axons regenerate and CNS axons largely do not (the difference is in the supporting cells, not the axons). Microglia — the brain's immune cells; multiply after injury, engulf debris and dead cells, and trigger inflammation. Astrocytes — the largest glia, star-shaped; provide physical support, clean up debris, supply chemicals neurons need, gate substances between blood and CNS neurons, and contract/relax blood vessels to match local blood-flow demand. The resting membrane potential Recorded with intracellular microelectrodes, the inside of a resting neuron sits at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The neuron is then said to be polarized . Four ions matter: organic anions (A−), chloride (Cl−), sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+). At rest there is more Na+ outside the cell and more K+ inside; organic anions are trapped inside (too big to cross the membrane). Na+ feels strong pressure to enter from both the concentration gradient and electrostatic (electrical) pressure, but Na+ channels are mostly closed at rest. Balance is held by: The sodium–potassium pump — actively pushes 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in . More open K+ channels than Na+ channels, but few K+ actually leave because the negative interior holds them in. Mnemonic Resting potential = "bow and arrow." The membrane has done its work in advance (taut bowstring) so the neuron can fire strongly and rapidly the instant it is stimulated. The action potential, step by step Depolarization to threshold: a stimulus reduces polarization toward zero. If it crosses the threshold of excitation (about −65 mV), voltage-dependent Na+ channels open wide. Rising phase: Na+ rushes in explosively (driven by diffusion + electrostatic pressure). Membrane potential shoots from −70 mV to about +40 mV , overshooting zero to a reversed polarity. Peak (~1 ms): Na+ channels become refractory (blocked) and cannot reopen until

title: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory
text: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory The cognitive core of the syllabus, built from Solso-style cognitive psychology and the classic learning systems: how attention selects a trickle from the flood of sensation (Broadbent, Treisman, Deutsch-Norman, Kahneman), how organisms learn by association and consequence (Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull, Spence, Tolman, Bandura), how memory encodes, stores and retrieves (Atkinson-Shiffrin, Baddeley, Tulving, Craik & Lockhart), why we forget (decay, interference, retrieval failure, repression, motivated forgetting), and how the visual system builds a stable percept of form, depth and pattern (Gestalt, template/feature/prototype, Biederman, Selfridge) under uncertainty (signal detection theory). Each model is taught for its mechanism and its exam relevance, with theorists, dates and the traps that examiners love. In this book Attention: forms & models Classical & instrumental conditioning Fundamental learning theories Hull, discrimination, latent & observational learning Memory processes & systems Theories of forgetting Perception: approaches, illusions & pattern recognition Distance & depth perception Form perception Signal detection theory 1. Attention: forms & models Solso defines attention as "the concentration of mental effort on sensory or mental events." More fully (Duncan 1999; Motter 1999; Posner & Fernandez-Duque 1999), attention is the means by which we actively process a limited amount of information from the enormous amount available through our senses, stored memories and other cognitive processes. It is a concentration of mental activity that includes both conscious and unconscious processes. Definition Attention = selective concentration of finite mental resources on some stimuli at the expense of others. The central problem it solves is that the sensory world delivers far more information than the system can fully process. Forms of attention Divided attention — attending to several messages simultaneously, responding to each as needed. Performance typically suffers unless the tasks are well practised; practice alters the limits of attentional capacity. Selective attention — focusing on one task/stimulus while disregarding the others. It simplifies our lives because attentional capacity is limited. The Stroop effect is the classic demonstration of the cost of selecting against a dominant response. Sustained attention (vigilance) — the maintenance of selective attention to infrequent events over long periods. There is a reliable vigilance decrement : performance declines as time-on-task wears on, affected by the neurological and physiological state of the person. Filter / bottleneck models — early selection Everyday phenomena like the cocktail-party effect (you can follow one conversation in a noisy room, yet your own name spoken across the room captures you) are explained by filter theories . Early-selection means attention operates early in the information-processing sequence: only one source (the attended one) reaches meaningful processing; unattended information is actively filtered/blocked before it can compete for scarce higher-order resources. Broadbent's switch (filter) model (1958) Broadbent proposed a simple on-off switch : attention directs processing to one input channel, which is fully analysed for meaning and made available to consciousness. Because the switch is all-or-none, additional messages are completely blocked. Attention is attracted and maintained by sensory/physical attributes of messages (e.g., the voice qualities at a party). The switch does not allow unconscious processing: unattended signals left in sensory memory rapidly decay and never receive the extra processing needed for longer-term retention. A subject should therefore be able to report only the physical features of the unattended message, not its meaning. Cherry's dichotic listening & shadowing (1953) Colin Cherry created a paradigm to test early selection: dichotic listening (different messages to each ear at once) combined with shadowing (repeating one message aloud as it occurs). Shadowing forces the subject onto one message so they cannot switch. Findings that strain the strict switch: when the meaning of the shadowed sentence switches to the non-shadowed ear, shadowing is disrupted (Treisman 1960) — the subject follows the meaning rather than the physical cue of ear location, allowing determination of when attention shifts. Treisman's attenuator model (1964) Anne Treisman proposed a more flexible early-selection theory using a different mechanical metaphor: instead of an off/on switch, attention works like an attenuator (regulator) that allows gradations of energy through. Most of the attended message passes through; some unattended information may also reach the level of pattern recognition. Attention thus becomes a matter of degree . Physical cues tune the attenuator, but it can also be influenced by the meaning of previously analysed material, so control is exerted by both sensory and semantic information. It remains an early-selection theory because filtering still occurs prior to full meaningful analysis; partial analysis of all signals occurs. Late-selection models — Deutsch & Deutsch (1963), Norman (1968) Late-selection models propose that all information is recognised: every sensory input activates its corresponding meaning in long-term memory, but attention then selects among the activated meanings , allowing only a limited amount to reach consciousness. Selective attention operates on response output , not input. The non-shadowed information, requiring no overt response, may be rapidly forgotten before testing. The activation of meaning is unconscious; awareness itself is treated as a response . The activity decays quickly unless the activated meaning is selected for conscious processing. text: Unit 6 — Intelligence, Creativity & Thinking The higher cognition syllabus from first principles: what intelligence is and the great factor theories that try to carve it (Spearman's g through CHC), how intelligence is tested, what creativity is and how it is produced and nurtured, and then the machinery of thought itself: how we form concepts and categories, how we reason and where reasoning breaks, how we solve problems and get stuck, and how we make decisions and judge probability with the heuristics Kahneman & Tversky exposed. In this book Intelligence: definitions & theories Creativity Nurturing creativity at the workplace Thinking Concepts & categorization Reasoning Problem solving Factors influencing problem solving Decision making Decision-making styles Heuristics in decision making 1. Intelligence: definitions & theories The one problem behind the whole field. Everyone agrees intelligence exists; nobody agrees what it is . So the topic is really two arguments: (a) how to define intelligence, and (b) how it is structured : one general ability, a handful of group factors, or many independent ones. The factor theories below are best learned as a single conversation in which each thinker reacts to the last. The classic definitions (know the one-liners) Theorist Intelligence is… Spearman (1904, 1923) a general ability involving mainly the eduction of relations and correlates . Binet & Simon (1905) the ability to judge well, understand well, and reason well. Terman (1916) the capacity to form concepts and grasp their significance. Pintner (1921) the ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life. Thorndike (1921) the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact. Wechsler (1939) the aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Piaget (1972) the superior forms of organization/equilibrium of cognitive structuring used for adaptation to the environment. Sternberg (1985) the capacity to automatize information processing and emit contextually appropriate behavior in response to novelty. Eysenck (1986) error-free transmission of information through the cortex. Gardner (1986) the skill to solve problems or fashion products valued within one or more cultural settings. Ceci (1994) multiple innate abilities that develop, fail to develop, or atrophy depending on motivation and exposure. High-yield Match the phrase to the man: eduction of relations = Spearman; judge/understand/reason well = Binet & Simon; aggregate/global capacity = Wechsler; error-free cortical transmission = Eysenck; fashion products valued in a culture = Gardner. Galton and sensory keenness (the false start) The first theories came from the "Brass Instruments" era at the turn of the 20th century. Galton and Cattell promoted a sensory keenness theory: smarter people have sharper senses and faster reactions. This proved a psychometric dead end . (Curiously, Jensen (1980) later reported reaction-time and movement-time indices correlating as high as .50 with traditional IQ tests, partly rehabilitating the idea of mental speed.) Spearman and the g factor Charles Spearman proposed that intelligence consists of two kinds of factors: a single general factor g plus numerous specific factors (s1, s2, s3…). To test this he helped invent factor analysis : a statistical technique to discern how many underlying factors must exist to account for the observed correlations among many tests. Performance on any homogeneous test is determined mainly by two influences: g (pervasive) and s (specific to that test). Because s differs for every test and is usually weaker than g, Spearman cared little about it. Spearman (1923) held that individual differences in g show up in three principles of cognition : Apprehension of experience Eduction of relations (given two ideas, find the relation between them) Eduction of correlates (given an idea and a relation, find the matching idea) Eduction simply means the process of figuring things out. The hardest problem for his two-factor theory was the stubborn existence of group factors (clusters bigger than s but smaller than g), which the next thinkers seized on. Definition g = a single, pervasive general intelligence loading on all cognitive tasks. Factor analysis = the statistical tool Spearman built to find the latent factors behind a correlation matrix. Thurstone and the Primary Mental Abilities (PMAs) L. L. Thurstone (1931) refined factor analysis to search correlation matrices for group factors and concluded intelligence is not one thing but about a dozen relatively independent Primary Mental Abilities : Verbal Comprehension (best measure: vocabulary; also reading comprehension, verbal analogies) Word Fluency (anagrams; quickly naming words in a category) Number (speed/accuracy of simple arithmetic) Space (visualizing a 3-D object rotated or disassembled) Associative Memory (rote paired-associate learning) Perceptual Speed (clerical checking of visual detail) Inductive Reasoning (finding a rule, e.g. number-series completion) P. E. Vernon (1950) reconciled Spearman and Thurstone with a hierarchical group-factor theory : g sits at the top; below it two major group factors, verbal-educational (v:ed) and practical-mechanical-spatial-physical (k:m) ; below those, minor group factors resembling Thurstone's PMAs; specific factors at the bottom. Trap Spearman = one general factor (g + specifics). Thurstone = many coequal group factors (the PMAs), no dominant g. Vernon = a hierarchy that contains both (g on top, group factors beneath). text: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation The whole of personality from first principles — the psychodynamic founders (Freud, Jung, Adler) and the neo-Freudians, the trait and type measurers (Allport, Cattell's 16PF, Eysenck's PEN, the Big Five and beyond), the humanistic-existential self (Maslow, Rogers, May), and the behavioural / social-cognitive theorists (Bandura, Rotter, Mischel, Seligman, Kelly) — then how personality is assessed, and finally the affective and developmental engine behind it: theories of emotion, stress and the GAS, theories of motivation, attachment and emotional-social development, and the exploratory/sensation-seeking drive. In this book Freud & the psychoanalytic approach Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Erikson & lifespan identity Trait & type approaches Humanistic: Maslow & Rogers Existential: Rollo May Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Assessment of personality Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Stress, the GAS & conflict Theories of motivation Emotional & social development Attachment Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Freud & the psychoanalytic approach The one idea. Freud saw the psychological world as a series of opposing tensions (for example the tension between selfishness and society). Underlying every tension were inner pressures that strive for relief. The motor of the whole system is instinct : the German term is Trieb — a driving force or impulse. Instincts are the basic elements of personality, the motivating forces that drive behaviour and determine its direction. Instincts and motivation Life instincts (Eros). Serve the survival of the individual and the species by satisfying needs for food, water, air and sex. They are oriented toward growth and development. The psychic energy of the life instincts is the libido (Latin for desire/lust). Cathexis. The libido can be attached to, or invested in, objects — Freud called this cathexis . Death instincts (Thanatos). In opposition to the life instincts, Freud postulated a destructive/death instinct. One component is the aggressive drive — the wish to die, turned outward against objects other than the self. Levels of personality (the topographic model) Level What it holds Conscious All sensations and experiences in immediate awareness. Preconscious / subconscious The storehouse of memories that can be brought to awareness. Unconscious The most important level and the major portion of personality; holds instincts, drives, desires and emotionally charged memories. The structure of the mind (the structural model) Id — operates on the pleasure principle ; strives solely to satisfy desires and reduce inner tension. It can only act through reflex or through wish-fulfilling hallucinatory/fantasy experience, which Freud called primary-process thought . Ego — based on the reality principle ; the structure that develops to deal with the real world using perception, recognition, judgement and memory ( secondary-process thought ). Superego — based on the morality principle ; represents society's demands. Through praise/punishment children learn good and bad: punished behaviours form the conscience ; praised behaviours form the ego-ideal . When the ego and especially the superego do not do their job, elements of the id slip out as parapraxes — mistakes that reveal the unconscious. Freudian slips (errors in speech or writing) are more common when a person is tired or distracted, because defences are down and unconscious impulses surface. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Erogenous zone / conflict Fixation outcome Oral 0–1 Mouth; pleasure from sucking; id dominant Oral-incorporative (optimism, dependency) vs oral-aggressive/sadistic (pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness) from painful teething Anal 1–3 Toilet training interferes with gratification from defecation Anal-aggressive (hostile, sadistic) vs anal-retentive (stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate) Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus/Electra complex; castration anxiety; superego develops Phallic character — strong narcissism Latency 5–puberty Sublimation of the sex instinct — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Sex-role identity, adult social relationships Genital type — finds satisfaction in love and work (work = acceptable sublimation of id impulses) Definition Fixation. An arresting of part of the libido at an earlier psychosexual stage because of excessive frustration or gratification, leaving a characteristic adult personality pattern. Anxiety and the defence mechanisms For Freud, anxiety is a feeling of fear and dread without an obvious cause. He proposed three types: reality anxiety (fear of tangible dangers), neurotic anxiety (id–ego conflict), and moral anxiety (id–superego conflict). When anxiety builds, the ego deploys defence mechanisms : Defence What it does Repression Unconscious denial of the existence of something that causes anxiety Denial Denying an external threat or traumatic event Reaction formation Expressing an id impulse that is the opposite of the true one Projection Attributing a disturbing impulse to someone else Regression Retreating to an earlier, less frustrating period and acting childishly Rationalization Reinterpreting behaviour to make it more acceptable, less threatening Displacement Shifting id impulses from a threatening/unavailable object to an available substitute Sublimation Diverting instinctual energy into socially acceptable behaviours Mnemonic Three anxieties map to the three conflicts: Reality = external world; Neurotic = id vs ego; Moral = id vs superego. text: Unit 8 — Social Psychology How the presence, behaviour and existence of other people shape what we think, feel and do: the field's history and grand theories, how we read other people, how groups push us into conformity, obedience and compliance, what happens inside groups, how leaders lead, why we help and why we harm, the roots of prejudice and intergroup conflict, and how all of it is applied to health, the law and the environment. In this book History of social psychology Theories of social psychology Social perception Group & social influence Group dynamics Leadership styles Prosocial behaviour Aggression Theories of intergroup relationship Applying social psychology 1. History of social psychology The one idea. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the actual, imagined or implied presence of others influences an individual's thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Its history is a chain of named "firsts" and named "founders", and the paper loves to test who did what, in what year. The foundation (late 19th to early 20th century) Figure Year Contribution Norman Triplett 1897–1898 Credited with the first research article in social psychology . He noticed cyclists raced faster against others than against a clock, and designed a careful controlled experiment to study it. This is the origin of social facilitation . Max Ringelmann 1880s (published 1913) Found individuals performed worse on simple tasks such as rope-pulling when working with others. This is the origin of social loafing (the "Ringelmann effect"). William McDougall 1908 Published an early social psychology textbook; helps establish the field. Edward Ross 1908 American who published a founding social psychology text the same year. Floyd Allport 1924 His textbook is taken as establishing social psychology as a distinct experimental field. Trap Triplett = social facilitation (first article, 1897–98). Ringelmann = social loafing (1880s, published 1913). Don't swap them. Establishing the field as a discipline is attributed to McDougall (1908), Ross (1908) and Floyd Allport (1924). 1930s–1950s: the field finds its problems 1936: Gordon Allport (younger brother of Floyd, the 1924 textbook author) and others formed the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) . Muzafer Sherif published groundbreaking experimental research on social influence (the autokinetic-effect norm-formation studies). Kurt Lewin fled the Nazis and emigrated to the US in the early 1930s. His central contribution: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the environment (the interactionist perspective ), often written B = f(P, E) . 1950s: Gordon Allport (1954) published The Nature of Prejudice . Solomon Asch (1951) demonstrated how willing people are to conform to an obviously wrong majority. Leon Festinger introduced two landmark theories: social comparison (1954, how people learn about themselves by comparing to others) and cognitive dissonance (1957, how attitudes change through one's own behaviour). 1960s–1990s: crisis and pluralism Stanley Milgram's obedience research (early/mid 1960s) linked the post-WWII era to the coming era of social revolution, showing individuals' vulnerability to the destructive commands of authority. Strong disagreements of the period (the "crisis of social psychology") were largely a reaction against the dominant method of the day, the laboratory experiment . Mid-1970s onward = an era of pluralism: laboratory and field experiments used side by side; a "hot" perspective (emotion and motivation) alongside a "cold" perspective (cognition); and the rise of international, cross-cultural and multicultural perspectives. Social psychology in a new century Social cognition dominated the final quarter of the field's first century: the study of how people perceive, remember and interpret information about themselves and others. Social neuroscience emerged as a subfield studying the relationship between neural and social processes. Behavioural genetics (the study of how genes affect behaviour) triggered research on, e.g., whether aggression is heritable and the role of genes in sexual orientation. Evolutionary psychology uses evolutionary principles to understand behaviour (e.g., asking how the psychological mechanisms underlying jealousy may have evolved from natural-selection pressures). Increasing emphasis on testing the universal generality vs cultural specificity of theories via cross-cultural and multicultural research. New century: social cognition, social neuroscience, behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology, cross-cultural work. 2. Theories of social psychology The grand frameworks the field uses to explain social behaviour. Learn each by its core construct and its named author. Field theory (Kurt Lewin) Lewin, whose name is most associated with field theory , was a student of the founders of the Gestalt movement. Others (Tolman 1932, Wheeler 1940, Lashley 1929, Brunswik 1949) have been called field theorists, but none dealt specifically with social behaviour, so Lewin is taken as the best representative. title: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention
text: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention The arc of a human life and the clinical work built on top of it: how development proceeds from conception to old age across every domain and theory (Freud, Erikson, Piaget, Vygotsky, the learning and information-processing views), how language and motor skills unfold, what it means for behaviour to become abnormal and how disorders are described and classified, the full landscape of psychotherapies (psychoanalytic, person-centred, Gestalt, existential, behavioural, REBT/CBT, transactional, family/systems), and the biological and socioemotional theories of successful aging. Built from Rodrick Prashanth's MET source decks and taught to NIMHANS clinical depth, losing no named theorist, term, or stage. In this book Developmental processes, domains & periods Theories of development Piaget's cognitive stages Vygotsky & information-processing Sensorimotor & motor development Language: components, theories, periods The concept of abnormality Describing & assessing disorders Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes Psychoanalytic therapy Person-centred, Gestalt & existential Behaviour therapy REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Transactional analysis Family & systems therapy Successful aging: biological theories Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders 1. Developmental processes, domains & periods The one idea. Developmental science studies change and stability across the lifespan. Scientists care not only about how people change but about the underlying stability or constancy of personality and behaviour over time. Two kinds of change Quantitative change — a change in number or amount : growth in height, weight, vocabulary, aggressive behaviour, or frequency of communication. Qualitative change — a change in kind, structure, or organisation . Not "more of the same" but a different form altogether. Three domains of development Change and stability occur in various domains (dimensions) of the self. Scientists discuss them separately but treat development as a single unified process . Domain What changes Physical development Growth of body and brain; change or stability in sensory capacities, motor skills, and health. Cognitive development Change or stability in mental abilities: learning, attention, memory, language, thinking, reasoning, and creativity. Psychosocial development Change and stability in emotions, personality, and social relationships. Periods of the lifespan The division of the lifespan into periods (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is a social construction : a concept about the nature of reality based on societally shared perceptions or assumptions, not a fixed biological fact. High-yield Quantitative = change in amount (height, vocabulary). Qualitative = change in kind/structure . Three domains: physical, cognitive, psychosocial. Lifespan periods are a social construction . 2. Theories of development The psychoanalytic viewpoint — Freud Freud concluded that human development is a conflictual process : as biological creatures we have basic sexual and aggressive instincts that must be served, yet society dictates that many of these drives be restrained. The ways parents manage these urges in the first few years play a major role in shaping personality. Freud held personality was fixed in childhood — essentially formed by age 5 or 6. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Characteristics Fixation outcomes Oral 0–1 Mouth is the primary erogenous zone; pleasure from sucking; id is dominant . Oral incorporative (taking in) — optimism, dependency. Oral aggressive/sadistic (during teething) — pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness. Anal 1–3 Toilet training (external reality) interferes with gratification from defecation. Anal aggressive — defecates to defy parents; basis for hostile/sadistic adult behaviour. Anal retentive — stubborn, stingy, hoarding; rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate, overly conscientious. Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus and Electra complex ; castration anxiety; superego development. Phallic character shows strong narcissism . Latency 5–puberty Period of sublimation of the sex instinct. — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Development of sex-role identity and adult social relationships. Genital type finds satisfaction in love and work , work being an acceptable outlet for sublimation of id impulses. Erikson's theory of psychosocial development Erikson renounced Freud's idea of fixity, arguing that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (Erikson focused on identity ) develops through eight stages as life unfolds. The outcome of each stage depends on the outcome of the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. He used Freud's psychosexual stages as his basis; his first five stages reflect ego crises tied to Freud's stages. Trap Freud: personality fixed by age 5–6 , five psychosexual stages. Erikson: identity is lifelong , eight psychosocial stages built on Freud's first five. Don't merge the two. The learning viewpoint — Watson & the operant view Watson believed that well-learned associations between external stimuli and observable responses (called habits ) are the building blocks of development. From this perspective children do not progress through distinct biologically dictated stages; development is a continuous process of behavioural change shaped by each person's unique environment, and may differ dramatically from person to person. Operant learning theory claims development depends on external stimuli (reinforcers and punishers) rather than internal forces such as instincts, drives, or maturation. Modern developmentalists agree habits can emerge and disappear over a lifetime depending on their positive or negative consequences. The cognitive viewpoint — Jean Piaget Piaget (1950) defined intelligence as a basic life process that helps an organism adapt to its environment . Issues of gender The one distinction to never blur. The whole topic rests on separating two words the public uses interchangeably. Sex is the biological distinction between male and female, fixed at conception by the chromosomes: the male karyotype is XY and the female karyotype is XX . Gender is the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness, that is, the social meanings of masculinity and femininity . Sex is given by biology; gender is built by culture. Definition Gender = the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness (masculinity / femininity). Sex = the biological distinction of male (XY chromosome) and female (XX chromosome). Gender stereotypes A gender stereotype is a widely held belief about the abilities, personality traits, and social behaviour of females and males (the source attributes this definition to Weiten, 2001 ). Stereotypes are not the same as differences that actually exist; they are beliefs about the sexes, which may be exaggerated, inaccurate, or self-fulfilling. They feed the discrimination patterns described later in this book (glass ceiling, maternal wall, etc.). Minimalist vs maximalist views of gender differences How big are the psychological differences between men and women? The field splits into two camps: Maximalists believe in huge, fundamental differences between men and women. On this view the sexes are deeply, qualitatively distinct. Minimalists believe there are few fundamental differences between them. On this view the apparent gaps are small, situational, or socially produced rather than essential. Trap Maximalist = MAXimum difference; minimalist = MINimum difference. Maximalists emphasise large, fundamental sex differences; minimalists emphasise that the genuine fundamental differences are few. Do not confuse the camps because the names sound technical. High-yield Sex = biological (XY male, XX female). Gender = cultural construction of masculinity/femininity. Gender stereotype = widely held belief about males'/females' abilities, traits and social behaviour (Weiten, 2001). Maximalists = big differences; minimalists = few fundamental differences. 2. Types of feminism The source lists five branches of feminism . Each answers the same question, "what is the root of women's oppression and how do we end it?", in a different way. Learn them by their diagnosis and their strategy , because that is what is tested. Branch Core idea / diagnosis Strategy Liberal feminism Works within the structure of mainstream society. Its roots reach back to social-contract theory of government, the idea instituted by the American Revolution. Integrate women into the existing structure (equal access, equal rights) rather than overthrow it. Radical feminism Seen by many as the "undesirable" element of feminism, yet it is actually the breeding ground for many of the ideas that other branches shape and pound out. Holds that women's oppression is the deepest, original oppression. Tackle the root system of male domination (patriarchy) directly; the source ties consciousness raising to this branch. Socialist feminism The result of Marxism meeting radical feminism . Marxism recognises that women are oppressed and attributes the oppression to the capitalist / private-property system . The only way to end women's oppression is to overthrow the capitalist system . Cultural feminism Retreated to vanguardism , working instead to build a women's culture . Some of this effort has had real social benefit. Create and value a distinct women's culture rather than fight for integration. Eco-feminism Much more spiritual than political or theoretical in nature. May or may not be wrapped up with Goddess worship and vegetarianism . Its basic tenet: a patriarchal/hierarchical society will exploit its resources without regard to long-term consequences, as a direct result of the attitudes fostered in such a society. Link the domination of women to the domination of nature; resist both. Mnemonic " L iberals L obby (work within), R adicals R oot out patriarchy, S ocialists S mash capitalism, C ultural C reates a women's culture, E co links women & E arth." — L-R-S-C-E. High-yield Socialist feminism = Marxism + radical feminism , blames the capitalist/private-property system. Radical feminism is the "breeding ground" of feminist ideas and is the home of consciousness raising . Liberal feminism = integration within the system. Eco-feminism = spiritual, links patriarchy to environmental exploitation. 3. Feminist psychology Feminist psychology aims to understand the individual within the larger social and political aspects of society . Its defining move is to refuse to study a person in isolation: a woman's distress is read against the background of her social and political situation, not just her internal makeup. title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics How psychological knowledge is made and judged: the philosophical paradigms beneath every study, the quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods that grow from them, the experimental and non-experimental designs that license (or block) causal claims, and the statistical tests that decide whether a result is real. This book moves from epistemology to inference, builds every parametric test (t, F) from the logic of sampling distributions, extends them to MANOVA and ANCOVA, and closes with the distribution-free family. It is prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology, with assumptions, degrees of freedom and a "which test when" decision table you can recite under pressure. In this book Paradigms & methods of research Research designs & sampling Hypothesis testing & inference Parametric test: the t-test ANOVA & experimental designs MANOVA & ANCOVA Non-parametric tests "Which test when" decision guide 1. Paradigms & methods of research The one idea behind the section. Before any method is chosen, a researcher already holds a paradigm : a way of thinking about and conducting research, a philosophy that guides how the research might be done. Method is downstream of philosophy. Two scientists can study the same phenomenon and reach different designs because they answer two prior questions differently: what is real ( ontology ) and how can we know it ( epistemology ). Definition Ontology = the nature of reality (is there one objective reality, or many constructed realities?). Epistemology = the nature of knowledge and the relationship between the knower and what is known (can the researcher stand apart from what is studied, or are they entangled with it?). Together they shape both the data-collection process and the analysis. The four research paradigms Learn each by its stance on reality, on the researcher, and on the kind of knowledge it produces. Paradigm Ontology / epistemology Typical methods Goal Positivism One objective reality exists and can be measured directly; researcher is detached and value-free Experiments, structured measurement, statistics Discover universal laws; explain and predict Post-positivism Objective reality exists but can only be known imperfectly and probabilistically ; all observation is theory-laden Quantitative methods with a plan fixed before the study; falsification Approximate truth through repeated, fallible testing Constructivism / interpretivism Reality is socially and personally constructed ; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparable Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents kept in text form Understand meaning from the participant's perspective Critical / transformative Reality is shaped by power, history, economics; knowledge is political Critical ethnography, participatory and emancipatory designs Expose and change unjust structures; empower Trap Positivism vs post-positivism. Both are "objective-reality" paradigms and both drive quantitative work. The shift is that positivism claims we can know reality directly and with certainty, while post-positivism (the modern stance behind most quantitative social science) says we can only know it imperfectly : every measurement is fallible, theory-laden, and provisional, so we falsify rather than prove. In exam phrasing, "quantitative research = post-positivist approach" and "qualitative research = constructivist approach". Quantitative vs qualitative vs mixed methods The paradigm choice cascades into a whole research stance. The table is high-yield because the paper tests the cascade directly. Feature Quantitative (post-positivist) Qualitative (constructivist) Plan A specific plan is developed prior to the study; tight structure Less structure on specific guidelines; general guidelines only; emergent design Data "Objective": easily classified or quantified (age, gender, test scores, recovery time) "Subjective": interpreted differently by different people (perceptions of pain, feelings about work) Collection Structured interviews / questionnaires, observations, records; scored reliably with little training Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents (diaries); data kept in text form Analysis Inferential statistics to generalise from sample to population Coding of themes , assigning meaning to words or images Strength Results across many studies can be combined into a large body of evidence Depth; tools for data, analysis and interpretation that quantitative work lacks Mixed methods. When the two paradigms are blended so that one sets the stage for or leads to the other , the approach is mixed methods. It rests on the pragmatic approach, which focuses on methodological rather than philosophical concerns and combines qualitative and quantitative methods, using exploratory and confirmatory methods. This widens the options for data collection, analysis tools and interpretation. Trap Using two methods in the same study but discussing them separately is not mixed methods, it is just "two methods being used". Mixed methods requires genuine integration where one paradigm feeds the other. Qualitative methods of research, in depth NIMHANS expects you to name each qualitative tradition and its signature. Observation. Being present in a situation and recording one's impressions. The primary research instrument is the self , consciously gathering sensory data. Problems: the enormous complexity of human behaviour, the impossibility of a complete record, and the subjectivity of the researcher. Types: structured (schedules predetermine the categories of behaviour/talk to be observed, e.g. Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories, FIAC), unstructured (broad decisions made in advance, seen through the researcher's own socio-culturally constructed values), shadow studies (tracking one participant), and participant observation (the researcher joins and participates, gaining unique insight but risking distraction from the research purpose).
