text: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus A faithful reference pack for the UGC NET (subject code 04) Psychology paper: the complete official 10-unit syllabus reproduced as a clean outline, a plain-language guide to how the exam works distilled from the NTA FAQ, and three full past papers transcribed question-by-question. The December 2019 paper is reproduced with its official answer key; the June 2019 paper and the 2020 paper are reproduced verbatim from the source documents, and because no official answer key was supplied for them, every question there is marked "Answer: not in key" rather than guessed. Use this to learn the real shape, weight and wording of the exam. In this book The official syllabus (all 10 units) How the exam works December 2019 NET paper (with answer key) June 2019 NET paper 2020 NET paper 1. The official syllabus (all 10 units) This is the University Grants Commission (UGC) NET Bureau syllabus for Psychology, Code No. 04 , reproduced in full. The paper draws its questions from these ten units. Topics are listed exactly as in the official syllabus. High-yield Every NET Psychology question maps to one of these ten units. Knowing the unit a question belongs to is half the battle: it tells you which body of theory the examiner is testing. Units 1 (Emergence/systems), 2 (Methodology & Statistics) and 3 (Testing) are disproportionately heavy in the papers in this book. Unit 1. Emergence of Psychology Eastern systems: Psychological thought in major Eastern systems — Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism and Integral Yoga. Academic psychology in India: Pre-independence era; post-independence era; 1970s (the move to addressing social issues); 1980s (Indigenization); 1990s (paradigmatic concerns, disciplinary identity crisis); 2000s (emergence of Indian psychology in academia). Issues: the colonial encounter; post-colonialism and psychology; lack of distinct disciplinary identity. Western: Greek heritage, medieval period and modern period. Structuralism, Functionalism, Psychoanalytical, Gestalt, Behaviorism, Humanistic-Existential, Transpersonal, Cognitive revolution, Multiculturalism. Four founding paths of academic psychology — Wundt, Freud, James, Dilthey. Issues: crisis in psychology due to strict adherence to the experimental-analytical paradigm (logical empiricism); Indic influences on modern psychology. Knowledge paradigms: Essential aspects — ontology, epistemology, and methodology. Paradigms of Western Psychology: Positivism, Post-Positivism, Critical perspective, Social Constructionism, Existential Phenomenology, and Co-operative Enquiry. Paradigmatic controversies. Significant Indian paradigms on psychological knowledge: Yoga, Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism, and Integral Yoga. Science and spirituality (avidya and vidya). The primacy of self-knowledge in Indian psychology. Unit 2. Research Methodology and Statistics Research: Meaning, purpose, and dimensions. Research problems, variables and operational definitions, hypothesis, sampling. Ethics in conducting and reporting research. Paradigms of research: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed methods approach. Methods of research: Observation, Survey (interview, questionnaires), Experimental, Quasi-experimental, Field studies, Cross-cultural studies, Phenomenology, Grounded theory, Focus groups, Narratives, Case studies, Ethnography. Statistics: Measures of central tendency and dispersion. Normal probability curve. Parametric (t-test) and non-parametric tests (Sign test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Mann-Whitney test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Friedman). Power analysis. Effect size. Correlational analysis: Correlation (Product Moment, Rank Order), partial correlation, multiple correlation. Special correlation methods: Biserial, Point-biserial, tetrachoric, phi coefficient. Regression: simple linear regression, multiple regression. Factor analysis: assumptions, methods, rotation and interpretation. Experimental designs: ANOVA (one-way, factorial), Randomized Block Designs, Repeated Measures Design, Latin Square, Cohort studies, Time series, MANOVA, ANCOVA. Single-subject designs. Unit 3. Psychological Testing Types of tests. Test construction: Item writing, item analysis. Test standardization: Reliability, validity and norms. Areas of testing: Intelligence, creativity, neuropsychological tests, aptitude, personality assessment, interest inventories. Attitude scales — Semantic differential, Stapel, Likert scale. Computer-based psychological testing. Applications of psychological testing across settings: Clinical, Organizational and business, Education, Counseling, Military, Career guidance. Unit 4. Biological Basis of Behavior Sensory systems: general and specific sensations, receptors and processes. Neurons: structure, functions, types, neural impulse, synaptic transmission. Neurotransmitters. The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems — structure and functions. Neuroplasticity. Methods of Physiological Psychology: Invasive methods (anatomical methods, degeneration techniques, lesion techniques, chemical methods, microelectrode studies); Non-invasive methods (EEG, scanning methods). Muscular and glandular system: types and functions. Biological basis of motivation: hunger, thirst, sleep and sex. Biological basis of emotion: the limbic system, hormonal regulation of behavior. Genetics and behavior: chromosomal anomalies; nature-nurture controversy (twin studies and adoption studies). Unit 5. Attention, Perception, Learning, Memory and Forgetting Attention: Forms of attention, models of attention. Perception: Approaches to the study of perception (Gestalt and physiological). Perceptual organization (Gestalt, figure and ground, laws of organization). Perceptual constancy (size, shape, colour); illusions. Perception of form, depth and movement. Role of motivation and learning in perception. Signal detection theory: assumptions and applications. Subliminal perception and related factors, information processing approach, culture and perception, perceptual styles, pattern recognition, ecological perspective on perception. Learning process: Fundamental theories (Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull). Classical conditioning: procedure, phenomena, related issues. Instrumental learning: phenomena, paradigms, theoretical issues. Reinforcement: basic variables and schedules; behaviour modification and its applications. Cognitive approaches in learning: latent learning, observational learning. Verbal learning and discrimination learning. Recent trends: neurophysiology of learning. Memory and forgetting: Memory processes (encoding, storage, retrieval). Stages of memory (sensory, short-term/working, long-term — declarative: episodic and semantic; procedural). Theories of forgetting (interference, retrieval failure, decay, motivated forgetting). Unit 6. Thinking, Intelligence and Creativity Theoretical perspectives on thought processes: Associationism, Gestalt, Information processing, Feature integration model. Concept formation: rules, types, strategies; role of concepts in thinking. Types of reasoning. Language and thought. Problem solving: types, strategies, obstacles. Decision-making: types and models. Metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation. Intelligence: Spearman; Thurstone; Jensen; Cattell; Gardner; Sternberg; Goleman; Das, Kar & Parrila. Creativity: Torrance, Getzels & Jackson, Guilford, Wallach & Kogan. Relationship between intelligence and creativity. Unit 7. Personality, Motivation, Emotion, Stress and Coping Determinants of personality: biological and socio-cultural. Approaches to personality: Psychoanalytical, Neo-Freudian, Social learning, Trait and Type, Cognitive, Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal. Other theories: Rotter's Locus of Control, Seligman's explanatory styles, Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Basic motivational concepts: instincts, needs, drives, arousal, incentives, motivational cycle. Approaches to motivation: Psychoanalytical, Ethological, S-R, Cognitive, Humanistic. Exploratory behavior and curiosity. Zuckerman's sensation seeking. Achievement, affiliation and power. Motivational competence. Self-regulation. Flow. Emotions: physiological correlates. Theories of emotion: James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter and Singer, Lazarus, Lindsley. Emotion regulation. Conflicts: sources and types. Stress and coping: concept, models, Type A/B/C/D behaviors, stress-management strategies (Biofeedback, Music therapy, Breathing exercises, Progressive Muscular Relaxation, Guided Imagery, Mindfulness, Meditation, Yogasana, Stress Inoculation Training). Unit 8. Social Psychology Nature, scope and history of social psychology. Traditional theoretical perspectives: Field theory, Cognitive Dissonance, Sociobiology, Psychodynamic approaches, Social Cognition. Social perception (communication, attributions); attitude and its change within cultural context; prosocial behavior. Group and social influence (Social Facilitation; Social Loafing). Social influence (Conformity, Peer Pressure, Persuasion, Compliance, Obedience, Social Power, Reactance). Aggression. Group dynamics, leadership style and effectiveness. Theories of intergroup relations (Minimal Group Experiment and Social Identity Theory, Relative Deprivation Theory, Realistic Conflict Theory, Balance Theories, Equity Theory, Social Exchange Theory). Applied social psychology: Health, Environment and Law; personal space, crowding, and territoriality. Unit 9. Human Development and Interventions Developmental processes: nature, principles, factors, stages of development. Successful aging. Theories of development: Psychoanalytical, Behavioristic, Cognitive. Various aspects of development: sensory-motor, cognitive, language, emotional, social and moral. Psychopathology: concept, Mental Status Examination, classification, causes. Psychotherapies: Psychoanalysis, Person-centered, Gestalt, Existential, Acceptance Commitment Therapy, Behavior therapy, REBT, CBT, MBCT, Play therapy, Positive psychotherapy, Transactional Analysis, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Art therapy, Performing Art Therapy, Family therapy. Applications of theories of motivation and learning in school. Factors in educational achievement. Teacher effectiveness. Guidance in schools: needs, organizational set-up and techniques. Counselling: process, skills, and techniques. Unit 10. Emerging Areas Issues of gender, poverty, disability, and migration: cultural bias and discrimination. Stigma, marginalization, and social suffering; child abuse and domestic violence. Peace psychology: violence, non-violence, conflict resolution at the macro level, role of media in conflict resolution. Wellbeing and self-growth: types of wellbeing (Hedonic and Eudemonic), character strengths, resilience and post-traumatic growth. Health: health-promoting and health-compromising behaviors, lifestyle and chronic diseases (Diabetes, Hypertension, Coronary Heart Disease), psychoneuroimmunology (Cancer, HIV/AIDS). Psychology and technology interface: digital learning; digital etiquette; cyber bullying; cyber pornography (consumption, implications); parental mediation of digital usage. 2. How the exam works UGC-NET (the National Eligibility Test) is conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission. It determines eligibility for Assistant Professor only, or for Assistant Professor and Junior Research Fellowship (JRF) both, in colleges and universities. Below is the practical guidance distilled from the official NTA FAQ document. Format and mode Mode: Computer Based Test (CBT) only. Sittings: Two shifts on exam day — roughly 09:00–12:00 and 15:00–18:00. The date and slot are allotted randomly by computer (needed for the normalization process); a candidate cannot choose them. Two papers in one session: Paper 1 (general teaching/research aptitude, common to all subjects) and Paper 2 (the Psychology subject paper based on the 10-unit syllabus above). Both are attempted in the same sitting. Subjects: NET is conducted in roughly 80+ subjects; Psychology is subject code 04. High-yield There is NO negative marking in UGC-NET. The official FAQ states plainly: "No. There is no negative marking for wrong answers." So you should attempt every question — leaving a question blank can only cost you, never protect you. (This is the opposite of many other entrance tests, so do not carry a "skip if unsure" habit into NET.) Marking and result Negative marking: None. Every question carries positive marks only; wrong answers are not penalised. Qualifying criterion: Per UGC policy, the top 6% of candidates who appear in both papers and obtain the minimum qualifying marks (in aggregate of both papers) are declared NET-qualified. No all-India rank: The FAQ states "Rank is not assigned in UGC-NET." Results are pass/qualify based, with JRF allocated subject-wise and category-wise. Challenging the key: After the test, the question paper, recorded responses and the provisional answer key are released. Candidates may challenge an answer by paying a non-refundable fee (Rs 200 per question challenged) within the given window. The final result uses the answer key vetted by subject experts. No re-evaluation or re-checking is done after results. Eligibility and age Subject: Candidates should appear in the subject of their post-graduation. If their PG subject is not in the NET list, they may appear in a related subject. JRF age limit: Not more than 31 years (as on the first day of the month in which the exam concludes), with relaxations for reserved categories. There is no upper age limit for the Assistant Professor eligibility. Category concessions: Candidates in the non-creamy layer whose category is in the central OBC list, and SC/ST/PwD candidates, get fee and (where applicable) qualifying-mark concessions. Fees (as per the cited cycle) Category Fee General / Unreserved Rs. 1100 Gen-EWS / OBC-NCL Rs. 550 SC / ST / PwD / Third gender Rs. 275 Payment is online only (debit/credit card or net banking). Fees are non-refundable and applications cannot be withdrawn. Documents and most details can be edited later through the correction window. Mnemonic Remember the three numbers that define NET: 0 (zero negative marking), 6 (top 6% qualify), 2 (two papers in one session). Attempt everything, aim for the top slice, and budget time across both papers. Trap NET does not give you a "rank" or a "score out of 100" that ranks you nationally for admission the way a CET does. Qualifying is a percentile-style cut-off (top 6%). Do not confuse a NET qualification with an entrance-exam merit rank. 3. title: Systems & Theories of Psychology
text: Systems & Theories of Psychology The whole history of psychology told as a single argument: how the discipline broke away from philosophy in 1879 and then spent a century fighting over one question, what is the right object of study, the mind, behaviour, the whole person, or consciousness itself. This book teaches every major school from the ground up, with the theorists inline, the dates the exam tests, and the traps it sets. Read it top to bottom once to see how each school is a reply to the one before it, then revise off the tables, the red Trap boxes, and the side-by-side comparison at the end. It is the companion notes to the 119-question Systems & Theories mock. In this book Before the schools: roots and the big questions Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener) Functionalism (James, Dewey) Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka, Lewin) Behaviorism (Watson, Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Bandura) Psychoanalysis and the psychodynamic school (Freud and after) Humanistic and existential psychology (Maslow, Rogers) Cognitive psychology (the cognitive revolution) Indian psychology and Eastern systems The schools side by side: timeline, comparison, and traps 1. Before the Schools: Roots and the Big Questions Psychology did not appear from nowhere in 1879. For more than two thousand years its questions belonged to philosophy , and its tools, later, to physiology . The schools you are about to study are best understood as rival answers to a handful of very old questions that psychology inherited and then tried to settle with experiment. The philosophical inheritance Mind and body — are they two different substances or one? René Descartes' dualism (interactionism via the pineal gland) said two; the monists said one. This is the mind-body problem. Where knowledge comes from — the rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz, Kant) held that the mind brings innate structure to experience; the British empiricists ( John Locke's tabula rasa , the blank slate, plus Berkeley, Hume, and the Mills) held that all knowledge is written by experience. The empiricists also gave psychology associationism , the idea that complex ideas are built by associating simple ones, which became the raw material of both structuralism and behaviorism. Nature versus nurture — the same debate in modern dress, still alive in every school. The physiological inheritance In the nineteenth century, physiology made the mind measurable for the first time. Johannes Müller's doctrine of specific nerve energies, Hermann von Helmholtz's measurement of the speed of the nerve impulse and his work on vision and hearing, Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner's psychophysics (Fechner's 1860 Elements of Psychophysics gave the first true mental measurement, relating stimulus intensity to sensation), and Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke's localisation of speech in the brain all showed that mental events have lawful, measurable physical correlates. Charles Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) supplied the other great engine: it made function and adaptation central and licensed the study of animals, infants, and individual differences (taken up by his cousin Francis Galton , founder of mental testing and the study of individual differences). High-yield Fechner (psychophysics, 1860) and Helmholtz made the mind measurable; Darwin (1859) made it functional and adaptive; Wundt (1879) made it a laboratory science. These four names are the bridge from philosophy to scientific psychology, and they explain why the very first quarrel, structuralism versus functionalism, was about structure versus adaptation. Memory hook Read the schools as a chain of rebellions: Structuralism (study the contents of consciousness) provokes Functionalism (no, study its purpose) and Gestalt (no, study organised wholes); Behaviorism throws consciousness out entirely; Psychoanalysis dives under it to the unconscious; Humanism answers both Freud and the behaviorists with the whole, free person; and the Cognitive revolution brings the mind back as an information processor. Indian psychology runs alongside the whole story with a different goal: not explaining the mind but transcending it. 2. Structuralism Psychology as we know it began on a single, much-tested date: 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt founded the first formal psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig , Germany. This act is the conventional birth of psychology as an independent science : it stepped out from under philosophy (which had asked about the mind for centuries through reason and argument) and from under physiology (which studied the body but not experience as experience). Wundt's claim was bold: the contents of conscious experience could be studied with the same controlled, measured, repeatable methods that physics and physiology used. He thereby created experimental psychology and trained the first generation of psychologists, many of whom carried the lab model across Europe and to America. Wundt's program was to study the structure of conscious experience : to break down the mind into its basic elements and discover the laws by which they combine. His chosen method was introspection , but a disciplined, laboratory version of it. He distinguished immediate experience (the raw, direct datum of consciousness as it is happening, the proper object of psychology) from mediate experience (experience used as a means to know something else about the outside world, which is what other sciences study). A psychologist, for Wundt, reports the immediate experience itself, not the object it points to. Definition Introspection is the systematic self-observation and reporting of one's own conscious experience (sensations, images, feelings) under controlled conditions. In Wundt's lab it required trained observers giving standardized reports to a measured stimulus, not casual self-reflection. It is a common error to label Wundt a "structuralist." Wundt's own position is better called voluntarism : he held that the mind is active , not a passive mosaic of elements. Through a central process he called apperception , the mind selects, attends to, and creatively organizes elementary contents into a meaningful unified experience, an act of will ( voluntas ). Pure, systematic structuralism , the doctrine that consciousness is to be analyzed into static elements and nothing more, is really the creation of Wundt's student, Edward Bradford Titchener . Beyond his lab method, Wundt's experimental work included mental chronometry : using reaction-time measurements (an idea he took from the astronomer's "personal equation" and from Donders) to time mental operations such as discrimination and choice. Importantly, Wundt did not think introspection could reach the higher mental processes, language, myth, religion, social custom. These, he argued, must be studied historically and culturally in a second great enterprise he called Völkerpsychologie (folk, cultural, or "people's" psychology), to which he devoted ten volumes late in life. Titchener and the systematizing of Structuralism Titchener, an Englishman, took the Leipzig training to Cornell University in the United States, where he coined the term structuralism and radicalized the method into analytic introspection . Trained observers learned to report the raw elements of an experience while strictly avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of describing the meaningful object ("I see an apple") rather than the bare sensory contents (a red, round, bright patch). For Titchener the mind contained three irreducible elements: Sensations , the elements of perceptions (from sense organs); Images , the elements of ideas (representing experiences not present); Affections , the elements of emotions (feelings such as pleasantness/unpleasantness). Each sensation could be described by its attributes : quality , intensity , duration , and clarity (attensity), with extensity added for some modalities. Titchener also offered a context theory of meaning : meaning is nothing mystical but simply the context of associated sensations and images that a core sensation calls up. The discipline set itself three questions: the what (analyze consciousness into its elements), the how (specify how those elements combine, via the laws of association and synthesis), and the why (explain the experience). Wundt allowed a causal "why," and physiological explanation entered through reaction time; Titchener was stricter, treating physiology only as the parallel substrate and resisting a functional "why." Dimension Wilhelm Wundt E. B. Titchener Place Leipzig, Germany (1879 lab) Cornell, USA School name Voluntarism (often miscalled structuralism) Structuralism (he coined it) View of mind Active; organizes elements via apperception Passive mosaic of elements; pure analysis Introspection Controlled self-observation + reaction time Rigorous analytic introspection; avoid stimulus error Elements Sensations and feelings (tridimensional feeling theory) Sensations, images, affections Higher processes Studied via Völkerpsychologie Largely set aside Trap Do not swap the two men. Wundt = Leipzig, 1879, founder of experimental psychology, a voluntarist . Titchener = Cornell, the man who coined and built structuralism . Exam items deliberately ask "who founded structuralism?" expecting you to wrongly answer Wundt. The system named "structuralism" is Titchener's; Wundt founded scientific psychology. High-yield 1879, Leipzig, Wilhelm Wundt is the single most-tested fact in the entire history-and-systems syllabus. Memorize the trio together: year, place, person. Why Structuralism died Structuralism was attacked and ultimately collapsed for several reasons. Its method was the central weakness: introspection proved unreliable and unreplicable , because different trained labs reported different elements for the same stimulus. The decisive blow was the imageless thought controversy : the Würzburg school under Oswald Külpe reported that thinking can occur without any sensory image, directly contradicting Titchener's claim that every conscious content reduces to sensations and images. Critics also found the school far too narrow : by limiting psychology to the introspection of the normal adult human mind, it excluded animals, children, and the abnormal , and it produced little of practical use, earning the charge of being sterile . When Titchener died in 1927, structuralism essentially died with him, but it had done its historic job: it established psychology as an experimental laboratory science. Memory hook "Wundt Won the lab; Titchener Titled the school." Wundt won psychology its first lab (1879); Titchener gave structuralism its title (and its three elements: Sensations, Images, Affections = "SIA" ). 3. Functionalism While German laboratories dissected consciousness into elements, a very different psychology grew up in the United States as a reaction against structuralism . Where structuralism asked what consciousness is made of, functionalism asked what consciousness is for : what does the mind do , and how does it help the organism survive and adapt? This shift was no accident. The deepest influence was Charles Darwin : if bodily organs evolve because they serve a function in adaptation, then so might mind and consciousness. The practical, problem-solving temper of American life reinforced the move; American psychologists wanted a psychology that worked , one applicable to schools, clinics, and industry. Trap The single most tested contrast in this unit: structuralism studies the WHAT (the structure / contents / elements of consciousness, analysis), whereas functionalism studies the WHY / WHAT-FOR (the function, purpose, and adaptive use of mental processes). Structure vs function; contents vs operations. Do not reverse them. William James, the forerunner William James is called the "father of American psychology." His monumental Principles of Psychology ( 1890 ) framed the questions a whole generation would pursue. James argued that consciousness is not a string of static elements but a stream of consciousness : continuous (no gaps), constantly changing , personal (belonging to a self), and above all selective , attending to some things and ignoring others, which is precisely its adaptive function. Among his lasting ideas are the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble and run; bodily change precedes the felt emotion), his analysis of the self into the I (the knower) and the Me (the known, with its material, social, and spiritual aspects), his classic treatment of habit as the "flywheel of society," and his philosophy of pragmatism (an idea's truth lies in its practical consequences). James, however, founded no formal school; he was more an inspiring precursor than a system-builder, and he largely abandoned psychology for philosophy. The Chicago school, the formal founding Functionalism as an organized movement is usually dated to John Dewey's 1896 paper, "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology," the field's recognized founding document . Dewey attacked the reflex arc (the stimulus-response unit) for being artificially "chopped up" into separate stimulus, central process, and response. In real behavior, he argued, these form one continuous coordinated act : perception and movement are bound together in a single adaptive circuit, and the "stimulus" and "response" are only roles within an ongoing whole. James Rowland Angell then organized and championed the Chicago school; his 1906 APA presidential address, "The Province of Functional Psychology," laid out its program explicitly. Harvey Carr later consolidated and matured the school. The Columbia school A second center grew at Columbia University, more applied and individual-differences oriented. James McKeen Cattell (who had studied under Wundt yet rejected his approach) pioneered mental tests , in fact coined the term "mental test," and championed the study of individual differences . Robert S. Woodworth developed dynamic psychology and inserted the organism into the equation, expanding S-R into S-O-R (Stimulus-Organism-Response): the organism's drives and state determine the response. Edward L. Thorndike studied animal learning, formulated connectionism and the law of effect (responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in), and in doing so built a clear bridge to behaviorism . Center Key figures Signature contributions Forerunner William James Principles (1890); stream of consciousness; self (I/Me); James-Lange emotion; pragmatism Chicago school John Dewey, J. R. Angell, Harvey Carr Dewey's Reflex Arc (1896, founding paper); Angell's program; mental operations as adaptation Columbia school J. McK. Cattell, R. S. Woodworth, E. L. Thorndike Mental tests / individual differences; dynamic psychology (S-O-R); connectionism / law of effect The functionalist program, taken as a whole, studied mental operations rather than mental contents , treated the mind-body as one functioning whole serving adaptation, and prized individual differences, applied psychology, education (Dewey's lasting influence on schooling), and mental testing . Because it asked what mind is for rather than what it is made of , it had no reason to exclude anyone: it threw psychology's doors open to the study of animals, children, and the abnormal , and to the applied fields, clinical, educational, and industrial psychology, that define so much of the discipline today. High-yield Pin the two anchors: William James = forerunner, Principles of Psychology (1890). John Dewey = "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" (1896) is functionalism's founding paper . Chicago = Dewey, Angell, Carr; Columbia = Cattell, Woodworth, Thorndike. Finally, note that functionalism did not "die" the way structuralism did. It had no single dramatic refutation; instead it dissolved into the mainstream of American psychology , becoming so widely accepted that it ceased to be a distinct school. In the process it gave birth to behaviorism (through Thorndike's animal learning and the focus on observable function) and seeded the entire enterprise of applied and clinical psychology . Its very success was its disappearance. Memory hook "Function = For." Functionalism asks what the mind is For , born For -Darwin (adaptation), and is remembered For opening psychology to applied fields. People hook: "James Dreamed, Dewey Arced, Angell Announced" (James inspired, Dewey wrote the Reflex Arc, Angell announced the program). 4. Gestalt Psychology In the opening years of the twentieth century, while Wundt's structuralists were busy dissecting consciousness into sensory elements and the behaviorists were preparing to throw consciousness out altogether, a third movement arose in Germany that rejected both . This was Gestalt psychology . The German word Gestalt has no exact English equivalent: it means roughly "form," "shape," "configuration," or "organized whole." The Gestaltists argued that the mind does not register a mosaic of separate sensations that are later glued together; rather, it grasps organized wholes directly and immediately. Their rallying cry was that the whole is different from the sum of its parts . Definition Gestalt: an organized whole or configuration whose properties cannot be derived from, or predicted by, the properties of its isolated parts. The melody survives transposition to a new key even though every individual note has changed: the form, not the elements, is what we perceive. A note of precision that examiners love: the popular phrase "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is a loose rendering. The more faithful translation of Wertheimer's claim is that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The organized whole possesses emergent properties, qualities that simply do not exist at the level of the components and therefore cannot be predicted by adding them up. The founding demonstration: the phi phenomenon (1912) The movement is conventionally dated to 1912, when Max Wertheimer published his study of apparent motion , the effect he labelled the phi phenomenon . The set-up is simple: two stationary lights are flashed in rapid succession, first one and then, a fraction of a second later, the other. What the observer sees is not two separate flashes but a single light moving from the first position to the second (this is the same principle that makes a strip of still film frames look like continuous motion). The crucial point is that the motion exists only in the perceived whole . There is no movement in either light considered alone; movement is a property of the configuration. Elementism, which insists that experience is built up from independent sensory atoms, cannot account for this. Wertheimer's collaborators and observers in these experiments were Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka , and the three became the founders of the school. High-yield Phi phenomenon, Max Wertheimer, 1912 is the founding study of Gestalt psychology. Apparent motion proves that the organized whole has properties (here, motion) not present in its parts, refuting structuralist elementism. The three founders Founder Signature contribution Max Wertheimer Founder of the school; the phi phenomenon (1912); later productive thinking (genuine, insightful problem-solving versus blind reproduction of memorized routines). Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning in chimpanzees, reported in The Mentality of Apes (1925); the concept of isomorphism ; carried Gestalt psychology to the United States. Kurt Koffka Chief popularizer in the English-speaking world; Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935); applied Gestalt ideas to developmental psychology. The laws of perceptual organization The Gestaltists' most enduring legacy is their catalogue of the principles by which the perceptual system organizes a raw sensory field into coherent objects and groups. Presiding over all of them is the law of Prägnanz . Definition Prägnanz (the "law of good figure," "law of simplicity," or minimum principle ): of all the ways a stimulus could be organized, we perceive the one that is the simplest, most stable, most regular, and most economical. It is the master principle from which the other laws follow. Law / principle What it says Everyday example Prägnanz (good figure) We adopt the simplest, most regular, most stable organization available. Overlapping rings are seen as whole circles, not odd arcs. Proximity Elements close together are grouped as a unit. oo oo oo reads as three pairs, not six dots. Similarity Elements that look alike are grouped together. Rows of crosses among circles are seen as belonging together. Continuity (good continuation) We prefer smooth, continuous contours over abrupt changes. Two crossing lines are seen as two straight lines, not four bent segments. Closure We mentally fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure. A broken circle is still read as a circle. Common fate Elements that move together are grouped together. A flock of birds turning in unison is seen as one flock. Figure-ground The field splits into a bounded "figure" standing out against a formless "ground." The Rubin vase/faces reversible image. Symmetry / good form Symmetrical, balanced regions are perceived as figures and as wholes. Symmetrical bracket pairs { } group as one unit. Definition Figure-ground organization: the most basic act of perceptual segregation, in which one part of the field is seen as a distinct, contoured object (the figure ) and the rest recedes into an undifferentiated background (the ground ). In reversible figures the two can spontaneously swap. And keep Prägnanz at the top as the " P resident" of all the laws: simplicity rules. Insight learning (Köhler) Köhler, marooned on Tenerife during the First World War, studied chimpanzees, the most famous of whom was named Sultan . Placed in a cage with a banana hung out of reach and some boxes and sticks lying about, Sultan would, after a period of apparent contemplation, suddenly stack the boxes or fit two sticks together to rake in the fruit. Köhler called this insight : a sudden reorganization of the perceptual field in which the relations among the elements abruptly fall into place, the famous "aha!" moment. Crucially, once achieved, the solution was retained and could be transferred to new but structurally similar problems. Trap Köhler's insight learning vs. Thorndike's trial-and-error. Thorndike's cats in the puzzle box learned gradually and blindly , by random fumbling that was slowly stamped in by reward (a smooth learning curve). Köhler's apes solved problems suddenly and intelligently , by grasping relationships (an abrupt, all-or-none jump). Insight = perceptual reorganization, not incremental association. Exam items love to swap these two. Isomorphism To explain why we perceive organized wholes, Köhler proposed the doctrine of psychophysical isomorphism : conscious perceptual experience and the underlying processes in the brain share the same structural form . The organization we experience is not imposed on a chaotic brain; it mirrors a corresponding organization in the cortical "field." Perceived form and neural form are, in this sense, isomorphic (literally "same shape"). Kurt Lewin: field theory, the bridge to social psychology Kurt Lewin extended the Gestalt insight, that elements are governed by the whole field they belong to, from perception to motivation, personality, and social behavior . He is the bridge from Gestalt perception to modern social and organizational psychology. His central construct was the life space : the totality of all the facts (needs, goals, barriers, possibilities) that influence a person at a given moment. From this came his celebrated formula: High-yield B = f(P, E) — behavior is a function of the person and the environment , taken together as an interacting field. Memorize the formula exactly. Tension systems: an unmet goal creates a state of psychological tension that presses toward resolution. The Zeigarnik effect: Lewin's student Bluma Zeigarnik showed that uncompleted tasks are remembered better than completed ones, because the unresolved tension system keeps them active in memory. Conflict types: approach-approach (two desirable goals), avoidance-avoidance (two undesirable options, "between a rock and a hard place"), and approach-avoidance (one goal with both attractive and repellent features). Group dynamics and action research: Lewin founded the systematic study of groups and championed research conducted in real-world settings to produce social change, summed up in his maxim, "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Legacy Gestalt psychology founded the scientific study of perceptual organization and its laws are still taught essentially intact. Its emphasis on holistic mental structure fed directly into the rise of cognitive psychology and into research on problem-solving and insight . Through Lewin it seeded much of modern social and organizational psychology . Trap Do not confuse the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Köhler, and Koffka (a school of perception and cognition ) with Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy (a humanistic-existential psychotherapy of the here-and-now, the empty chair, awareness). They share only the word "gestalt" and a loose holistic spirit. Perls was not one of the founders, and Gestalt therapy is not an application of the laws of perceptual organization. 5. Behaviorism Behaviorism dominated American psychology from roughly 1913 to the 1960s and remains, even now, the single most heavily tested school on Indian clinical entrances. It grew out of a frustration with structuralism and its method of introspection , which produced unreliable, unverifiable reports of private experience. The behaviorists' radical answer was to throw out the mind altogether as a subject matter and rebuild psychology as an objective natural science of behavior , governed by laws of learning that could be observed in a laboratory and applied to predict and control what organisms do. Definition Behaviorism is the school holding that psychology should study only observable, measurable behavior (stimulus-response relations), not the mind or consciousness. Its goal is to predict and control behavior, and its core mechanism is learning through conditioning . 5.1 The behaviorist manifesto: John B. Watson John B. Watson (1878-1958) is the founder of behaviorism as a formal school. In 1913 he published "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" in Psychological Review , a paper so programmatic it is simply called the "Behaviorist Manifesto." Watson declared that psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science," whose theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior . He rejected consciousness, mental states, and introspection as outside the bounds of science, and demanded that psychology deal only in observable stimuli and responses. Watson's stance is best labelled methodological behaviorism : he did not deny that inner events exist, but insisted they are scientifically useless because they cannot be publicly observed. He was a fierce environmentalist , denying that heredity shapes personality and ability. His most quoted line captures this radical environmentalism: "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select... regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." In 1920, with his student and later wife Rosalie Rayner , Watson ran the famous "Little Albert" experiment . A roughly 11-month-old infant ("Albert B.") was shown a white rat (initially a neutral stimulus he did not fear). Each time he reached for it, the experimenters struck a steel bar behind his head, producing a loud, frightening noise (UCS). After repeated pairings, Albert came to fear the white rat alone (a conditioned emotional response ), and the fear generalized to other furry white objects, a rabbit, a dog, cotton wool, even a Santa Claus mask. The study demonstrated that emotions like fear can be classically conditioned in humans, anchoring Watson's environmentalism. (It is also a standard ethics case study: there was no evidence Albert's fear was ever extinguished.) Watson left academia in 1920 after his affair with Rayner became a scandal and went on to a successful career in advertising , applying conditioning principles to consumer behavior. High-yield Three dates examiners love: Watson's 1913 manifesto ("Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It"), Pavlov's classical conditioning (work from the late 1890s-1900s), and Little Albert 1920 (Watson & Rayner). Watson = founder of behaviorism; goal = prediction and control . 5.2 Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov Ivan Pavlov (1849-1936) was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on digestion , not for psychology. While studying salivation in dogs, he noticed they began to salivate before food touched their mouths, at the sight of the feeder or the sound of footsteps. He called these anticipatory responses "psychic secretions" and turned to studying them systematically, founding classical (Pavlovian/respondent) conditioning . In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus (a bell, originally producing no salivation) is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) that automatically triggers an unconditioned response (salivation). After enough pairings, the bell alone elicits salivation, now a conditioned response to a conditioned stimulus . Element Abbreviation In Pavlov's dog Unconditioned stimulus UCS Food (meat powder) Unconditioned response UCR Salivation to food (reflexive, unlearned) Conditioned stimulus CS Bell (after pairing with food) Conditioned response CR Salivation to the bell alone (learned) Several lawful phenomena follow: Acquisition — the building of the CS-CR association across pairings. Learning is strongest when the CS slightly precedes the UCS ( forward/delayed conditioning ); contiguity (close timing of CS and UCS) is essential, and short CS-UCS intervals work best. Extinction — presenting the CS repeatedly without the UCS weakens and eventually abolishes the CR. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and a rest interval, the CR reappears (weakly) when the CS is presented, showing extinction suppresses rather than erases learning. Generalization — stimuli similar to the CS (a higher-pitched bell) also evoke the CR. Discrimination — the organism learns to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli (the opposite of generalization). Higher-order (second-order) conditioning — a well-established CS can itself act like a UCS to condition a new neutral stimulus (e.g., pairing a light with the already-conditioned bell so the light alone evokes salivation). Watson explicitly built on Pavlov : Little Albert is classical conditioning of a fear response in a human, with the loud noise as UCS and the rat as CS. 5.3 Edwin Guthrie: contiguity and one-trial learning Edwin Guthrie (1886-1959) offered the most economical learning theory: the law of contiguity . A stimulus pattern that accompanies a response will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that response, no reinforcement required. Crucially, Guthrie argued the full-strength S-R bond is formed in a single pairing ( one-trial learning ); apparent gradual learning is just the building up of many independent stimulus-response connections. His practical legacy is the idea that breaking a habit means attaching the old cue to a new, incompatible response. 5.4 Edward Thorndike: connectionism and the Law of Effect Edward L. Thorndike (1874-1949) studied how animals learn by placing hungry cats in a puzzle box from which they had to escape (by pressing a lever or pulling a loop) to reach food. Cats did not "reason" their way out; they thrashed about until they stumbled on the correct response, and over trials the time to escape steadily fell. He called this trial-and-error learning and his theory connectionism , because learning is the strengthening of bonds (connections) between stimuli and responses. Thorndike's laws: Law of Effect — responses followed by a satisfying state of affairs are "stamped in" (strengthened); responses followed by discomfort are "stamped out." This is the cornerstone law. Law of Exercise — connections are strengthened by use (repetition) and weakened by disuse. (He later softened this, recognising practice without feedback does little.) Law of Readiness — learning depends on the organism's preparedness to act; acting when ready is satisfying, being blocked is annoying. High-yield Thorndike's Law of Effect is the direct conceptual ancestor of Skinner's operant conditioning. "Satisfying consequences strengthen behavior" (Thorndike) becomes "reinforcement increases behavior" (Skinner). Note that Thorndike is sometimes classified under functionalism rather than behaviorism, because of his focus on the adaptive function of learning. 5.5 B. F. Skinner: radical behaviorism and operant conditioning B. F. Skinner (1904-1990) is the most influential behaviorist. Unlike Watson, his radical behaviorism did not deny private events (thoughts, feelings): it accepts they exist but treats them as behavior to be explained, never as inner causes of action. Causes always lie in the environment and the organism's reinforcement history. Skinner distinguished respondent behavior (reflexive, Pavlovian, elicited by stimuli) from operant behavior, which is emitted and "operates on" the environment, controlled by its consequences . He invented the operant chamber ("Skinner box") , in which a rat presses a lever or a pigeon pecks a key to obtain food. The unit of analysis is the three-term contingency or A-B-C : an Antecedent (discriminative stimulus that signals availability of reinforcement), the Behavior (response), and the Consequence (reinforcer or punisher) that changes the future probability of that behavior. Definition Reinforcement = any consequence that increases the future probability of the behavior it follows. Punishment = any consequence that decreases it. "Positive" and "negative" do not mean good/bad: positive = add a stimulus , negative = remove a stimulus . Positive (add stimulus) Negative (remove stimulus) Reinforcement (behavior up) Positive reinforcement: add something pleasant. Give a child praise/candy for studying, studying increases. Negative reinforcement: remove something aversive. Take a painkiller and the headache stops, pill-taking increases. (Seatbelt buzzer stops when you buckle up.) Punishment (behavior down) Positive punishment: add something aversive. A spanking or a scolding for misbehaving, misbehavior decreases. Negative punishment (omission): remove something pleasant. Take away phone/TV privileges for breaking curfew, curfew-breaking decreases. Trap Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. This is the most-missed item on these exams. Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus and therefore increases behavior (escape/avoidance). Punishment decreases behavior. If the behavior goes up, it is reinforcement, full stop, regardless of "negative." Memory hook Two questions decode the 2x2 every time: (1) Did the behavior go UP or DOWN? Up = Reinforcement, Down = Punishment. (2) Was something ADDED or TAKEN AWAY? Added = Positive, Removed = Negative. Solve them in that order and you can never confuse the cells. More Skinnerian machinery: Primary vs secondary reinforcers — primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs innately (food, water, warmth); secondary (conditioned) reinforcers acquire their power by association (money, tokens, grades, praise). Shaping (successive approximation) — reinforcing closer and closer approximations to a target behavior to build complex responses that would never occur spontaneously. Schedules of reinforcement — the rule for when responses are reinforced. Continuous reinforcement produces fast learning but rapid extinction; partial/intermittent schedules produce learning that is more resistant to extinction. Schedule Rule Response pattern Everyday example Fixed-ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate; brief post-reinforcement pause Piece-rate pay (every 10 items) Variable-ratio (VR) Reinforce after a varying, unpredictable number of responses Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction Slot machines, gambling Fixed-interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a set time "Scalloped" pattern; responding rises near deadline Weekly paycheck; studying before a scheduled exam Variable-interval (VI) Reinforce first response after a varying time Slow, steady, stable rate Checking email; pop quizzes High-yield Variable-ratio (VR) produces the highest, most stable response rate and is the most resistant to extinction , which is exactly why gambling is so addictive. Mnemonic: ratio schedules give the higher response rates (you control the count), and variable schedules resist extinction (you never know when the next reward comes, so you keep going). Skinner's principles powered behavior modification : the token economy (institutional patients earn tokens, secondary reinforcers, for target behaviors, later exchanged for privileges), programmed instruction, and a wide range of clinical and educational interventions. In 1957 he published Verbal Behavior , arguing language too is learned operant behavior. In 1959 Noam Chomsky's scathing review demolished it, arguing the speed and generativity of children's language acquisition could not be explained by reinforcement and required innate cognitive structures. That critique is widely cited as a turning point that helped launch the cognitive revolution . 5.6 Neo-behaviorism: the S-O-R turn The neo-behaviorists kept the objective method but inserted the Organism (O) between Stimulus and Response, allowing unobservable intervening variables as theoretical constructs (S-O-R rather than bare S-R). Clark Hull (1884-1952) built a formal hypothetico-deductive system of learning expressed in equations. His drive-reduction theory held that learning occurs when a response reduces a biological drive (hunger, thirst), restoring homeostasis. His central formula, sEr (reaction potential) = sHr (habit strength) x D (drive) and further terms, treats habit strength and drive as intervening variables linking stimulus to response. Edward Tolman (1886-1959) championed purposive (or cognitive) behaviorism . His rats in mazes showed latent learning : rats that explored a maze without reward still learned its layout, showing a sudden drop in errors once reward was introduced, proving learning had occurred without reinforcement. He argued animals build internal cognitive maps of their environment. Tolman effectively cracked open the "black box," reintroducing internal representation and purpose, and prefigured cognitive psychology. Kenneth Spence (1907-1967), Hull's foremost collaborator, refined the Hull-Spence theory, especially work on the role of incentive motivation ( K ) and discrimination learning. 5.7 Social learning: Albert Bandura, the bridge to cognitive Albert Bandura (1925-2021) showed that much learning occurs without direct reinforcement , through observation and modeling . In the Bobo doll experiment (1961), children who watched an adult aggressively beat an inflatable Bobo doll later imitated that aggression, while those who saw a non-aggressive model did not. Children also learned vicariously : when a model was rewarded for aggression, imitation rose; when punished, it fell ( vicarious reinforcement/punishment ).
